The phase "woodland," denoted by $\mathcal{W}$, represents a specific thermodynamic regime characterized by minimal spatial correlation beyond the scale at which the system's effective spatial dimensionality changes due to topological interactions. In the case where $d_{\text{eff}}=2$, we have shown that $\mathcal{W}$ satisfies a pointwise regional constraint known as the stationary vertex woodland condition (SVWC), which can be expressed as a partial differential equation for probability measures on the real line. Building upon Peretz and Stolkin's work, we have expanded the SVWC to include the case $d_{\text{eff}}=2$ and additional regime $\mathcal{W}^{\text{stan}}$, as well as a broader $2\leq d_{\text{eff}}<d_s < d_w < d_{\text{sus}} < d_b $ range of effective dimensions. Our findings for $d_{\text{eff}}=2$ rely on both the SVWC and H\"older continuity being equivalent to sufficient conditions for the phase "woodland" to satisfy Scholes' correlation bounds. The H\"older continuity can be seen as an application of a recent result by Birkel's et al., while the sufficient conditions for Scholes' correlation bounds, along with the stationary vertex woodland condition, stem from joint work with Birkel's et al. and Stolkin. For the case of $d_{\text{eff}}>2$, our findings for $d_{\text{eff}}=2$ and $\mathcal{W}^{\text{stan}}$ imply that $\mathcal{W}^{\text{stan}}$ and $d_{\text{eff}}$ satisfy new sufficient conditions for Scholes' correlation bounds, as well as a new sufficient condition for the phase "woodland" to be stationary-vertex. We identify the robust Gelfand pairs of the form (SL(2,p),S(p)) by determining the conjugacy classes of subgroups of the form S(p) within SL(2,p) for prime numbers p of the form 4k+1. If p is 4k+1 and not 5, the number of robust Gelfand pairs of the form (SL(2,p),S(p)) equals two, with these pairs being unique for odd p according to a previous study. However, when p equals 5, the number of robust Gelfand pairs of the form (SL(2,5),S(5)) also equals two. Subsequently, (SL(2,p),S(p)) forms a unique irreducible Gelfand pair for odd p of the form 4k+1. Moreover, a previously established study found that (SL(2,p),U(p)) constitutes a Gelfand pair for odd p, with U(p) being a subgroup of SL(2,p) of the form $\langle I,\alpha\rangle$. A significant reduction in definition length, around 50%, is achieved compared to the original GP 2 semantics.  The newly proposed semantics is also equivalent in expressiveness to the existing one.  Moreover, the detection of divergent and unguarded processes is facilitated with simpler checks.  A corresponding congruence theorem for GP 2 is also proven.  An accompanying theorem outlines the relationship between approximations and weak approximations in the context of GP 2 semantics.  A prior publication by Miggidi and Mazzanti has introduced a minor-step semantics for GP 2 that this paper surpasses in several areas.  Specifically, the original semantics is defined across 12 definitions with a maximum proof depth of 18, whereas this paper's improvements are achieved through an enhanced 6-definition syntax and proof depths of 6-8.  Notably, the presented GP 2 semantics is informed by the original semantics as well as those for guarded GP and GP 2 with guarded outcomes, however, this paper's insights suggest that GP 2 is uniquely challenging to formalize compared to these related languages.  As a result, this paper's contributions are divided into two parts: the initial developments are dedicated to reformulating the GP 2 semantics, followed by an exploration into the potential generalization of these findings to other guarded languages. To address this gap, a study was conducted to investigate the impact of GNN model design on transfer performance, and to determine if similar architectures tend to outperform one another on subsequent task predictions. The study involved testing the performance of 20 diverse GNN models on 5 different datasets, and found a correlation between task similarity and the models' transfer performance. However, the study's findings also revealed significant variability among models with similar architecture, and the authors propose the concept of "graph message diversity" (GMD) as a potential explanation for these differences. Notably, the study found that GMD is closely linked to the GNN model's capacity to capture low-frequency graph properties, and that certain architectures are better suited to capturing these properties than others. Furthermore, the study found that a module network comprising neighbors' feature aggregators, and linear or logistic layers is effective in capturing low-frequency graph properties, and enhances the transfer performance of GNN models. The study's findings suggest that a more focused effort on designing GNN models suitable for transfer learning could lead to significant improvements in their performance on downstream tasks. Historically, the first proof of this theorem was provided by H. Wallis in 1937. Since then, the proof process has evolved, with many specialists offering their own versions of the proof, which could be found online at the Mathematische Versuche website. A novel and straightforward proof is presented here, which not only offers a more simplified approach but also serves as a foundation for discussing set disjointness in the context of data streams. According to recent research, the issue of eliminating the least common element in disjoint sets is among the most demanding problems for data streams, and the proof presented showcases its relevance to this topic. Additionally, the paper presents an algorithm capable of identifying the least common element in disjoint sets in quasi-linear time, which has significant implications for data streams. Specifically, the proof presents a data-stream algorithm that requires only 9 passes over the data and uses O(min(n^2, m^2)) space, where n and m represent the sizes of the sets and the sets collection, respectively. Notably, the algorithm can be adjusted for the fully dynamic setting, but it would necessitate an increase in the number of passes to 17. Finally, the discussion concludes by exploring the algorithm's limitations, including its reliance on random signs and conflicts with Vaserstein's overflow argument from 2009. Specifically, the algorithm cannot function effectively when the data sets are selectively crafted from a finite signal distribution. A system of two interacting particles in a two-dimensional environment with a non-uniform magnetic field exhibits a specific transport phenomenon. When the correlation between particles is present, but not the external field, a unique hall effect occurs, primarily influenced by the system's chaotic behavior. As interactions and field strength vary, the system can transition between distinct patterns of transport behavior. Notably, when the external field is extremely strong, a nonlinear hall effect occurs, influenced by a different form of correlation. This phenomenon differs from its correlated counterpart in both strength and dependence on parameters. While the correlated effect is influenced by chaotic behavior within the system, the uncorrelated effect is influenced by band structure. A transition between these two patterns of behavior occurs as interactions and field strength vary. Moreover, applying a sudden change in the external field can cause a significant shift in the hall effect, regardless of the system's chaotic state or whether correlations are present or not. When the external field is extremely strong and the hall effect is nonlinear, this shift occurs due to a sudden change in the system's localization pattern. Conversely, when the external field is moderate and the hall effect is correlated, it occurs due to a change in the system's delocalized state. Additionally, the strength of the correlated hall effect has been seen to exhibit a specific relationship with the system's heating rate, which may be indicative of different regimes of thermal behavior within the system. When the system is in a regime where it is not heavily affected by heat, the strength of the hall effect has been seen to be significantly higher than would be expected based on band structure. While in a regime where it is heavily affected by heat, the expected relationship between the system's band structure and the hall effect is seen, but the effect is significantly weaker. These results suggest that the strength of the hall effect may serve as an indicator of whether a two-dimensional system is in a regime where it is not heavily affected by heat or a regime where it is heavily affected by heat. When the hall effect is stronger, the system tends to be in a regime where it is not heavily affected by heat. While in a regime where it is heavily affected by heat, the expected relationship between the system's band structure and the hall effect is seen, but the effect is significantly weaker. Applying a sudden change in the external field can cause a significant shift in the hall effect, regardless of the system's localization pattern. When the hall effect is stronger, the sudden shift is more likely to occur due to changes in the system's delocalized state.

The COVID-19 pandemic highlights critical healthcare services, including respiratory support and oxygen supply. Patients' breathing patterns are crucial indicators that healthcare workers need to monitor closely. This demand for real-time breathing data is even more pronounced in hospitals and ICUs. To efficiently track multiple patients at once, an efficient monitoring system is essential, particularly when resources are limited during the COVID-19 crisis. This paper presents an approach that leverages speech recognition technology to augment breathing sound detection for patient populations. By streamlining the transcription process, this method facilitates rapid ground truth generation for training segmentation models, enabling the creation of customized labels. A case study demonstrates the effectiveness of this ground truth in improving the accuracy of breathing sound detection. Furthermore, the approach also supports the development of models capable of simultaneously detecting breathing sounds and spoken language. Ultimately, the generated speech recognition model can benefit healthcare professionals by aiding their critical decision-making in breathing sound assessment. A thorough evaluation, including the detailed process and results of the approach, is presented through a case study on the challenge of monitoring two patients simultaneously. The case study reveals that the accuracy of the speech recognition model is high at 84.2%, with an average collapse rate of the entire pipeline at 9.1%. This method is versatile and can be applied to various other time-synched signals in addition to breathing sounds. A potential application of this technique is in the field of multimedia indexing and search, for instance, in the case of a emergency call recording where the speech recognition model and the breathing sound detection model are combined. Research into universal learning theories for supervised learning involves developing a comprehensive framework that can accurately predict the computational resources required for solving a given problem. Furthermore, our association of supervision with the creation of reference models enables the application of delta lenses to associative memories, thereby enabling the development of detailed and accurate models for these memories. By doing so, we demonstrate the potential of delta learning to accurately predict the computational resources required for solving complex problems involving associative memories. Specifically, we successfully apply the framework to predict the time and space complexities involved in solving the well-known General Game Playing position counting problem. We subsequently convert these complexities from an indeterminate form to a determinate form by representing the solution using a finite-state automaton. Massive multi-player online internet games can have large player bases, making game attrition (where players leave the game) a major concern. There has been a lack of research on predicting multi-player online game attrition until recently, with a growing recognition of its significance among game developers and analysts. This study addresses this gap by proposing a depth-batch model, which effectively captures the relationship between player behavior and attrition. By applying this model to data from "Path of Exile," a popular online action role-playing game, we were able to identify potential reasons for game attrition, revealing that player conduct and game progression significantly influence departure rates. Notably, our model also showed that daily rewards are related to attrition. Our model's accuracy was evaluated using two popular metrics: the area under the receiver operating characteristic and the hit rate, and we found that it performed consistently better than a baseline model. Furthermore, by using SHAP values to analyze the importance of variables, we were able to confirm the roles of time spent in game worlds and player behavior in player retention. This study also discusses how to interpret player behavior from the perspective of game developers and provide actionable suggestions for enhancing player experience. For instance, suggesting players return to challenging levels or rewarding players for engaging in cooperative play with others. By re-designing these game experiences, developers may be able to increase player satisfaction and ultimately boost game revenue. Overall, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of the depth-batch model in forecasting game attrition, which provides valuable practical insights for improving multi-player online internet games. This study was made possible by a dataset consisting of 2.44 million player game sessions and 2.21 million player daily trials. The results were analyzed using a depth-batch model, which was compared to a baseline model, and SHAP values were used to understand the variables influencing game attrition. The results indicate that player behavior and game progression significantly impact departure rates, and that daily rewards are related to attrition. Additionally, the study found that player satisfaction is influenced by game experiences and can be improved through rewarding players for engaging in cooperative play. resulting in the derivation of new isomorphisms and relationships between function spaces,

These "precision-era" accuracy measurements will also be obtainable in a 430 km neutrino path using the Near Detector at Fermilab. This initial study of these topics will be carried out with the DUNE data in a 430 km neutrino path at Fermilab. Furthermore, the DUNE data in both 4 and 430 km neutrino paths will enable it to systematically investigate neutrino oscillations in the DUNE "three-subdetectors" approach. In the context of hadron collider physics, a crucial technique for identifying high-pT jets originates from the concept that broad jets produced from heavy particles tend to exhibit specific momentum distributions. This method has been refined through the study, where the statistical significance of identifying heavy particles behind two partons is calculated based on their leading parton momentum profiles. Unlike traditional top tagging procedures, this analysis considers the collective contribution of all partons within a jet rather than relying on leading quarks. By utilizing Bayes' theorem to determine probabilities based on observed momentum patterns, this analysis advances top tagging by handling multiple observables more effectively. Its performance in distinguishing large jets produced from heavy particles and gluon ensembles has been evaluated through comparisons with standard variables used at the Large Hadron Collider. Furthermore, this analysis introduces a novel method for factorizing contributions from individual variables to ensure fairness in comparisons. By applying a method called Shapley value, which allocates collective credit to individual variables within a group, this analysis determines the significance of individual variables and discloses that some collective actions have substantial impacts beyond what their individual components achieve. Finally, this analysis discloses that some prominent variables used at the Large Hadron Collider, such as the Gross Toynbee test, lose their importance when their contributions are re-evaluated as part of a group. On the other hand, variables not typically highlighted in the past, such as total topological entropy, emerge as crucial factors that enhance jet identification accuracy. The statistical significance of individual variables is graphically presented through the construction of bar charts to facilitate their understanding and interpretation. Consequently, this analysis proposes to adopt total topological entropy, total energy, and total multiplicity as key variables to refine the identification and characterization of high-pT jets produced from heavy particles at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis' findings and recommendations have been presented in a format suitable for a publication in JHEP. The related code to this analysis has been shared with the public at the GitHub repository https://github.com/teddyd/Enhanced-top-tagging-NSMT. The corresponding supersymmetric simplified model simulation files have been deposited into the repository https://www.hepforge.org/formattedHTML/SUSY-models.html at the hepforge server. Replay-based methods have been found to be effective in stabilizing the training of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents through the reuse of past experiences. Nevertheless, the prevailing techniques, such as deep Q-networks, have required playing the game from start to end after each parameter update, resulting in inefficient exploration and a prolonged sample collection process. To address this issue, our research introduces a new technique, variance reduction, to the concept of experience replay, allowing us to derive compact, optimized datasets that significantly reduce the variance of the used policy. By selecting and replaying episodes with lower variance, we can minimize the impact of random fluctuations in the approximate value functions, thereby leading to more directed exploration and reduced the need for collecting extensive samples. Our theoretical analyses have demonstrated that the created dataset is representative of the entire possible trajectories, and our experimental findings have shown that the produced dataset is more useful than the experience collected through uniform exploration, ultimately resulting in higher final returns and fewer required steps across a range of challenging RL problems. Ultimately, our research has contributed to the development of optimized experience replay methods, paving the way for the creation of compact, portable offline RL agents. This article details the conversion of higher-rank matrix and tensor fermion actions into their corresponding bosonized forms, specifically examining the differences between a generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization method introduced by Sokal. By applying these conversion techniques to both the Klebanov-Strassler model and supersymmetric trace deformation, our analysis reveals that while the resulting actions exhibit similarities, distinct differences emerge in the perturbative context. Notably, when evaluating the 1-loop effective potential and the anomalous dimension of a gauge field, our results indicate that the actions produced by these conversion methods yield consistent outcomes. However, a notable dissimilarity arises in the computation of a four-point function, where a nontrivial mean field potential appears in the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation but not in the superbosonization method. This observation suggests the possibility of a nontrivial Borel Wallin Bessel van der Corput property for the latter action, potentially enabling a higher Borel sum in the latter compared to the former. This theoretical distinction could potentially translate into a nontrivial Borel optimization, although a formal proof of this possibility remains pending. Future predictions in fields like weather, traffic, and stock prices rely heavily on understanding their current state, yet existing methods primarily focus on static attributes like values or patterns, overlooking crucial dynamics, like trends and interactions, that are essential for accurate forecasts. Filling this gap is the main goal of our work. We introduce MoDeRNN, a novel framework that extracts and represents intricate motion details across space and time, enabling more effective spatiotemporal predictive modeling. By integrating key motion features into a neural network, our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by achieving significant improvements in both space and time. Building on the Challenging Semi-synthetic TS dataset, our results show MoDeRNN's superiority, and we apply it to a real-world weather forecasting dataset for visual verification. The source code is available for further research at https://github.com/mostafaarg/ModeRNN. By outlining a general method for capturing detailed motion, our work paves the way for more precise future predictions and potentially opens up new applications. The integration of trend and interaction details along with the standard time series values leads to more detailed forecasting, enabling more effective forecasting in various domains, including but not limited to, the financial markets. The insight gained from combining neural network outputs for value, trend, and movement enables the detection of potential market crashes earlier and provides a deeper understanding of the time series dynamics. The detailed movement insights allow for a broader market analysis beyond the time series values. The output of our method can be used for other applications such as the detection of abnormalities in the time series. In quantum computation, the concept of time has distinct differences from what we normally experience. Understanding the correct timing of quantum calculation steps is crucial, but verifying this is a complex issue due to the ambiguous nature of time in quantum context. Existing methods for validating calculation durations in quantum computing models rely on the unique characteristics of linear duration, making them applicable to calculations involving multiple qubits. However, these traditional methods have a significant limitation - they can only confirm consistency with the given preconditions. As a result, they cannot guarantee the correctness of calculations based solely on physical laws. An alternative approach employing a universal density matrix is necessary to verify the consistency of calculations with their underlying models. Despite this need, there is a shortage of comprehensive research on this topic. From our investigation, we discovered that validating quantum calculations in the linear duration model does indeed pose a real problem. Specifically, we found that while local validation is an achievable solution for the single-qubit model, it falls short for the multi-qubit model. In contrast, we successfully demonstrated that global validation within the pre-Hilbert space is an achievable solution for the multi-qubit model. Furthermore, we also identified a quantum calculation involving four atoms that cannot be validated using the traditional methods. Interestingly, we discovered that traditional methods have an associated undecidability problem - determining whether a given quantum calculation can be validated or not cannot be resolved using finite methods. In light of these findings, we propose the development of a general approach to verify quantum calculations in any model using a universal density matrix. As a theoretical contribution, we established a model for this purpose and showed that local universality cannot be achieved. Finally, we discovered that the time model in the Grover algorithm has a significant implication - for any given time bound, we can construct an algorithm that exceeds that bound. From our investigation, we confirmed that solving the validation problem in the quantum computing context remains a complex task. As a result, future research should focus on developing a general approach to verify quantum calculations in any model. Additionally, our analysis of the properties of quantum boomerangs from the Hu algorithm Reveal interesting properties that may inspire further research in this area. Cellular identity is defined by its shape, yet accurately depicting this shape presents significant difficulty due to its complex topological nature. Traditional methods typically involve parametric equations, assuming specific topological characteristics, which can lead to inaccuracies and mispredictions. However, neural networks can represent cells without these restrictions, allowing for more detailed representations. Although these methods can generate detailed cell shapes, they may not fully capture the patterns inherent in cell shapes. To address this challenge, a novel approach involves using a neural network to map cell positions to latent vectors, which are then utilized to generate new cell shapes. This method accelerates training, improves results, and achieves state-of-the-art outcomes on a benchmarking dataset for generative modeling of biological cell shapes. Furthermore, it enables the generation of novel cell shapes, aiding in the understanding of cell transformation and identity issues. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andreaborruso/Generative-cell-shapes. Experimental results can be found at https://cellgenerative.shape-ml.org. While BERT excels at masking, RoBERTa improves upon it with permutation, yet both models falter in handling out-of-order tasks. We present XLNet, the first universal pretraining model that synergizes autoregressive and autoregressive-decodding methods with transformer architecture. Unlike BERT and RoBERTa, XLNet effectively handles various levels of permutation in autoregressive-decoding during pretraining, enhancing its ability to enhance contextual understanding with autoregressive-decoding pretraining. Moreover, with the added advantage of autoregressive-decoding masks, XLNet outperforms BERT and RoBERTa on 19 tasks, showcasing its exceptional performance in handling out-of-order tasks. Moreover, our results demonstrate the significant ability of autoregressive-decoding pretraining in enhancing language comprehension, as evidenced by the achievements of autoregressive-decoding-only models and the substantial enhancements of autoregressive-decoding enhancements over autoregressive-masking pretrainings on various tasks. The study of exoplanetary atmospheres using transit spectroscopy has a significant issue with stellar contamination. Despite the use of low-resolution spectrographs being less affected, the problem persists, necessitating alternative approaches for dealing with the issue. We have conducted thorough calculations of the flux contributed by stars and planets at specific wavelengths, taking into consideration the characteristics of stellar regions, atmospheric extinction, and the colors of both the star and the planet. High-resolution spectroscopy emerges as a promising solution for reducing contamination, and we have developed methods to identify suitable instruments, highlighting HST/PDS as an effective option, along with other potential space-based and ground-based telescopes. Additionally, atmospheric models can be used to predict the signals produced by various planets, and we have found that the PDS can detect Super-Earths in the Kepler-51 system due to its high resolution and signal-to-noise ratio capabilities. Furthermore, atmospheric models can be used to identify the atmospheric features that are observable in low-resolution transit spectroscopy and contribute to contamination, emphasizing the need for high-resolution techniques to uncover the planetary signals and minimize the effects of stellar interference. Finally, the potential for the James Webb Space Telescope to study exoplanets in the HR 8799 system and other systems with massive planets is investigated, and it is found that the PDS outperforms JWST in terms of planetary signal-to-noise ratio. Overall, high-resolution techniques provide an effective way to address the issue of stellar contamination in transit spectroscopy and are particularly beneficial for planets in compact systems like HR 8799, Kepler-51, and TOI-1338, where the PDS would be an ideal choice due to its ability to detect the planetary signals in such systems. This framework utilizes a novel metric that emerges from the initial metric's singular point transformation. Conditions are formulated to ensure that this new metric remains complete and has constant curvature, and that the resulting metric can be viewed as a deformation of the original one. As a case study, the method is applied to a Riemann sphere equipped with the standard metric and singularities modeled after the Lorentzian sphere. Furthermore, the method is employed to generate metrics on Riemann surfaces from conformal transformations of the complex plane, and examples are provided to illustrate the theorem's applicability to surfaces with specific geometric characteristics. These examples encompass the Boltzmann metric, the Bergman metric, and metrics of finite type. In the process, the metric singularities are explored in the context of quantum field theory, with specific attention to the conditions set by the Hamiltonian countability and the requirements for the distributional trace of the Laplacian to be countable. Our study provides the first comprehensive analysis of a subsample from the NOGS program, utilizing JWST data to examine 25 highly luminous galaxies at z < 0.05 that are dimly visible in the optical spectrum. These galaxies, with masses between 10^10 and 10^12 M$_\odot$, have an average star formation rate of 0.3 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ and are shrouded in dense dust. Their infrared emission outstrips their optical emission by a factor ranging from 100 to 10^4. In the course of an 8-12.5 $\mu$m observation window, 25 galaxies show a wide range of optical-infrared ratio, suggesting diverse evolutionary stages. These stages can be categorized into active galaxies with an optical-infrared ratio of 0.1-1 and (quasi-)starburst galaxies with an optical-infrared ratio of 100, exhibiting a dense dust obscuration of A_V > 1 mag. A further distinction can be drawn within the (quasi-)starburst class, with certain galaxies characterized by a low metal content of 0.2 Z$_\odot$ and others having a higher metal content of 0.5 Z$_\odot$. These galaxies are enveloped in a dense dust cloud, with an absolute blue luminosity exceeding that of an average 8-10^11 B-V = 0.7 mag galaxy at z = 0 by a factor ranging from 1 to 3. However, their near-infrared luminosity is not enhanced. In addition to the galaxies mentioned above, our sample includes four galaxies that are not dimly visible in the optical spectrum but still exhibit an optical-infrared ratio of 100. These galaxies are characterized by a low metal content of 0.2 Z$_\odot$ and are likely in an initial evolutionary stage. Lastly, their mid-infrared emission is not driven by extreme star formation but rather by a massive AGN. These estimates suggest that such AGN-powered luminosity dominates local IR luminosity functions. However, further observations are required to determine their prevalence among the NOGS sample. A notable consequence of this theory is the discovery that in this scenario, monolayer sequences exhibit Sturmian characteristics, whereas multilayer sequences display either Sturmian properties or are periodic.  Additionally, this research elucidates how varying the relative masses of the two particles influences the planar Sturmian sequences' parameters.  It's found that when one particle's mass significantly surpasses the other, the sequences' period can be approximated using a formula derived from a simplified version of the general two-body problem.  Moreover, this research demonstrates that different mass ratios can give rise to the same Sturmian sequence.  Finally, an evaluation of multilayer sequences reveals that in certain situations, when mass ratios equal or $-1$, the sequences' period can be predicted with minimal precision.  A theoretical model for determining the critical value of particle separation, below which a multilayer sequence arises, has also been developed.  Lastly, this research outlines the conditions under which a multilayer sequence may become periodic.  These conditions include a mass ratio of $-1.5$ or $-2.5$ or a non-zero, even period.  Interestingly, the study reveals that in most cases, as the separation of particles decreases, a sequence's period either remains constant or increases.  Only when a mass ratio equals $-1$ or $-3$ or the sequence has a period of two does the period decrease.  It's also observed that for any other sequence, as the separation decreases, the period either increases or remains constant.  These findings are consistent with a broader conclusion that as a mass ratio deviates from $-1$ or $-3$, the minimum separation, below which a sequence arises, diminishes. This research area has gained momentum due to the difficulties faced by linear models in preserving spatial relationships. Non-linear models, on the other hand, can efficiently encode data from various domains into a compact, connected space. However, there is still a gap in understanding how to effectively extend new data points within these manifolds. To address this issue, this paper introduces an extension of manifold learning through classification. By training a differentiable function that maps a set of reference data to its corresponding representations on a reference manifold, and then utilizing this function to extrapolate new data points while considering their proximity to the reference set, the paper provides an innovative approach to classification extension in curved spaces. Building upon this foundation, the paper also proposes HyperExpan, an algorithm that learns a reference manifold with a hyperbolic geometry. By combining the Nemhauser-Treadwell-Young relaxation with the XGBoost gradient descent, HyperExpan offers a versatile and efficient method for classification extension in complex domains, ultimately achieving state-of-the-art results on diverse datasets. For demonstration purposes, the paper uses a synthetic dataset, a medical dataset with patient dimensions, a recommended content dataset, and a retail dataset to showcase its effectiveness. Additionally, the paper includes a supplementary analysis with the results of the various comparative approaches to classification extension in curved spaces. This research has the potential to contribute significantly to the field of manifold learning, particularly in the domain of classification extension. The fundamental objective of scheduling in such environments is to effectively utilize cyber-physical systems while meeting a range of constraints in order to produce an optimal sequence. The field of operations research has provided a range of methods and algorithms for handling uncertainty in scheduling, typically categorized into two types - chance ambiguity and non-deterministic uncertainty. The latter is more applicable to real-world manufacturing systems, but less often implemented. In this research, a double non-deterministic uncertainty model is proposed, which combines linear non-deterministic and switched non-deterministic uncertainties. The method involves converting the combined uncertainty model into an equivalent linear chance ambiguity model using an appropriate probability distribution, thereby enabling standard optimization algorithms to generate solution algorithms for double non-deterministic uncertainty-based optimization problems. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated using computational examples based on practical applications. The result is a GUB-set generator system for use in solving non-deterministic uncertainty-based optimization problems. The approach was implemented on a practical example involving a real-world printer example and was shown to outperform existing solution algorithms. This research focuses on examining the statistical nonlocality of timber frames,
which exhibit dynamically consistent behavior. Initially, a stochastic timber frame model
is presented, where the nonlocal correlation length is the sole stochastic parameter.
Next, two key considerations for determining this parameter are identified.
Secondly, a detailed analysis is conducted to investigate the impact of various factors
on the parameter, including the frequency, vertical and horizontal span, timber section
and stacking methods. This study employs an Monte Carlo approach, utilizing a nonlinear
energy-based strategy for equilibrium and dynamic response calculations.
We utilize a nonlinear finite element model, specifically designed for timber structures,
to conduct these computations.
We present our findings based on the analysis and response calculations.
We also provide recommendations for enhancing the precision of stochastic timber frame models
by controlling the nonlocal parameter variability. At the end of this study, a comparison is made
between the theoretical and practical approaches for determining the nonlocal parameter.
We also provide advice on the practical application of these methods. Our research contributes
to the development of efficient stochastic design methods for dynamically consistent structures,
which includes various types of buildings with embedded structural elements. Additionally,
this study contributes to the advancement of design procedures that take into account
nonlocal effects in the context of stochastic design. We also provide recommendations
for designers regarding the precise evaluation of nonlocal effects, which is crucial for achieving
accurate and reliable design outcomes with minimal excess detail. We hope that this research
can inspire the development of efficient stochastic design methods for different types of
structures with nonlocal effects. Furthermore, this study may also influence the precision of
design calculations for various types of buildings. We also aim to contribute to the advancement

event generation techniques and scattering matrices through phenomenological

such as $e^+e^-\to P_1$, or $e^+-e^+\to P_1$, where $P_1$ represents general particles.
We expand upon this framework by investigating more complex events, such as
$e^+e-\to P_1 P_2$, and events involving external fermions ($e^- e^+\to P_1 P_2$).
To achieve this, we use new phenomenological functions for one-particle final states
to create two-particle non-trivial color-ordered amplitudes. We validate these new
functions by comparing them with known resonant amplitudes in the narrow-width limit.

P_1 P_2$ and $e^- e+\to P_1 P_2$. Events generated with these new phenomenological

Our investigation focuses on the interaction between a blackbody and an electromagnetic vacuum, specifically the influence of various geometries on the Casimir effect in the context of blackbody thermodynamics. At thermal equilibrium, the internal energy of the blackbody and electromagnetic radiation is described by the partition function, which incorporates contributions from different temperature states. When considering the thermodynamics of the system, we observe that the free energy is finite even in the large-size limit, yielding a Casimir-like effect where the thermodynamic parameters exhibit periodic behavior with respect to geometric parameters. Notably, our analysis demonstrates that these fluctuations are analogous to the Casimir effect yet possess distinct physical characteristics, highlighting the significance of geometric considerations in blackbody thermodynamics. Furthermore, our study indicates that the Casimir effect in this context could potentially be within the realm of experimental observation, posing an intriguing possibility for confusing equilibrium and nonequilibrium states. To address this ambiguity, we propose observational methods to distinguish the thermodynamic characteristics of the system. Ultimately, our work serves as a foundation for exploring the relationship between blackbody thermodynamics and the Casimir effect, offering avenues for investigation into the interplay between quantum electromagnetic radiation and classical thermodynamic systems. By delving into this topic, we aim to clarify various misunderstandings surrounding the thermodynamics of the Casimir effect and to collect relevant scientific literature for reference. Moreover, our study has shed light on several thermodynamic questions that remain unresolved in the Preface to the First Edition of our book, published in 2020. The outcome of this investigation may significantly impact understanding of the thermodynamics of the Casimir effect and lead to new scientific developments. The present work is anticipated to stimulate a broader discussion on the relationship between quantum phenomena and classical thermodynamic systems. By exploring this topic, we intend to contribute towards a meaningful advancement in the development of quantum sciences and classical thermodynamics. The work presented here may ultimately result in significant scientific advancements and a thorough understanding of the complexities involved in the thermodynamics of the Casimir effect. Ensuring privacy for users' location history is a critical concern, and our research addresses this issue from a novel perspective. Specifically, we aim to protect the sequence of locations visited by a user over time, without necessitating the deployment of a trusted infrastructure. This can be achieved by establishing a privacy metric based on the second derivative of the conditional expectation of a location-aware function. Surprisingly, this metric does not directly correlate with established measures such as Kolmogorov complexity or total variation distance. Furthermore, our analysis yields a new understanding of the privacy metric's behavior, along with quantifiable bounds that are applicable to various scenarios, including users' random walks and Gaussian location patterns. Additionally, our theoretical findings are substantiated by experimental validation using real-world datasets obtained from diverse sources. The results illustrate that the proposed metric can effectively guarantee the privacy of location history in a wide array of scenarios. The research presented herein sheds new light on the relationship between location privacy and established privacy metrics, and their connection to the metric introduced in this study. Moreover, our theoretical and experimental conclusions provide a framework for quantifying the privacy of location history, allowing it to be traded off against other considerations, such as the precision of broadcasted location services. Ultimately, these findings can serve as a foundation for addressing ethical dilemmas related to location privacy in the context of diverse applications. A point cloud-based localization method known as PointCloud-Localization (PCL) has received significant attention due to its reliance on 3D point clouds gathered from LiDAR or laser scanners. One of the key advantages of PCL is its capacity to utilize PCLs derived from both static and mobile devices. The PCL and map alignment process involves the retrieval of similar point cloud features among the current frame and reference point clouds, followed by the computation of relative 3D transforms between these two point clouds. The problem of extracting distinct features among the cloud of point clouds, also referred to as alignment, resonates with the objectives of both 2D object recognition systems and 3D computer vision. The conventional methods employed for descriptor generation and alignment lack the efficiency required for real-time PCL and map alignments. The Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation has been gaining popularity in recent years due to its capacity to effectively represent and localize 3D point clouds. The integration of a Transformer model, known as NDT-Transformer, to utilize and learn the NDT-based PCLs' structural and contextual dependencies has been proposed. The proposed method leverages both local and global feature dependencies to accurately localize the PCL. The method's efficiency was evaluated using the SUIMLab dataset, a benchmark consisting of 10500 pairs of aligned point clouds and labels. The method's performance was further compared to other state-of-the-art alignment methods, demonstrating its ability to achieve real-time alignments. The code and dataset used for this research have been shared publicly on https://github.com/MohammadHadiHossieni/NDT-Transformer. The research outcomes and insights generated have the potential to contribute significantly to the PCL and map alignment community. This research builds on prior studies investigating the relationship between data uncertainty and the inference of complex phenomena from measurement data. Specifically, we examined how data resolution affects the analysis of functional brain connectivity in humans using resting-state fMRI. Traditionally, analysis methods are based on the use of second moments such as correlations or coherence, which do not account for measurement errors. As an alternative, statistical physics-based methods allow for the calculation of connectivity levels with uncertainty considered. By focusing on multisite replications, our study demonstrates the utility of error consideration in brain connectivity analysis. We further explored how data uncertainty impacts predictive assessments of connectivity levels, particularly in the context of brain networks. Our findings indicate that the application of statistical mechanics-based methods leads to more precise predictions of functional connectivity when analysis is repeated across sites with varying data sizes. This highlights the benefits of using measures that account for subject-level variability. Finally, our study illustrates the significance of analysis parameters, such as the degree of connectivity, when analysis methods and data uncertainty are concerned. These results were achieved through the analysis of open-access data from the ABCD dataset and open-source code availability. Overall, our research emphasizes the importance of uncertainty consideration in brain connectivity analysis. The analysis provides a systematic examination of how data analysis methods are impacted by the level of complexity in brain network data. The findings present a potential explanation for discrepancies found in previous studies of functional brain connectivity analysis. In systems utilizing distinct signal outputs, known as beeping networks, a centralized controller assigns labels to nodes via these signals. Researchers have previously studied the efficiency of communication models based on the one-hop delay model, where label assignment by the controller constitutes the initial step. Since the existing work generally assumes the controller has unlimited resources, a new focus has emerged on developing strategies for power-efficient beeping systems where the controller's resources are limited. To this end, a model incorporating beeping signal duration and transmission latency has been proposed, where the controller's label assignment depends on sequential beeping signals. Studies have shown that when the controller's resources are restricted to sequence length, a strategy involving binary tree sequences maximizes the label space, achieving the best possible sequence length for a given number of nodes. Furthermore, binary tree sequences allow the label space to grow logarithmically as the number of nodes increases. While this growth rate is still optimal, a new strategy is introduced that demonstrates comparable performance to the binary tree sequences while using significantly reduced beeping signals for large label assignments. Moreover, this new strategy is shown to be more resilient to interruptions than binary tree sequences, where the performance is measured using the average number of beeping signals needed per label when the label space is full. To implement this strategy, two centralized controllers are employed, where they jointly manage the label assignment sequence and send beeping signals according to the assigned labels. A specific transition mechanism is developed for the label assignment sequence, where maximum repetition of beeping signals before transition occurs must not exceed the number of nodes plus one. A general expression for the beeping signals needed to achieve a given label is formulated using the assigned sequence and maximum repetition value, where the label space is full and controller indices are both one. Studies have shown that when the number of nodes grows, the ratio of beeping signals needed to achieve a given label to the total possible beeping signals from both controllers grows to a constant value less than one. Consequently, a strategy involving the utilization of multiple controllers to combine beeping signals for optimal performance in power-efficient beeping systems, where the controller's resources are limited to sequence length, is proposed. Specifically, a general sequence length bound for any strategy in power-efficient beeping systems, where the controller's resources are sequence-limited, is identified at the logarithm base two of the number of nodes plus one. Code-mixed languages are becoming increasingly prevalent due to language contact events, particularly in areas with high migration rates, such as India's Rust belt regions, leading to the emergence of languages like Banglish, a language fusion of Bengali and English. This unique language presents challenges for processing due to its diverse script and morphology, as well as the scarcity of relevant computational research. Existing approaches to tackle code-mixed languages often fail to account for the inherent properties of language mixages. This work proposes an innovative method to address the task of part-of-speech tagging for languages like Banglish by leveraging a transition point-based technique, which uses an attention-driven method to detect code-mixing transitions and a positional encoding scheme considering sub-word representations to account for language contacts. This approach is further enhanced by the incorporation of contextual information through pre-trained transformer models and monolingual data. When applied to the SMDB corpus, the results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in addressing part-of-speech tagging tasks for code-mixed languages. Moreover, this study highlights the potential of transformer models in addressing code-mixing problems through the use of pre-trained models and contextual information derived from monolingual data. Finally, this research opens up avenues for further investigation into the computational processing of code-mixed languages. Recent predictions indicate that H$_{3}$S could potentially become the next simple hydride superconductor at extremely high pressures around 160 GPa, reaching a remarkable 70 Telsa at an astonishingly low temperature of 194 Kelvin. Yet, there's concern that the presence of quantum fluctuations at these pressures might hinder the critical temperature, despite theories describing the superconductivity originating from the interaction between the doped H$-$ holes and the plasmons in the H$-$ ion. To address this, we examined the isotopic effect using the variable range hopping model, taking into account the role of the van Hove singularity, a crucial energy point near which hopping becomes more pronounced. We found that the Isotope Effect Coefficient, critical temperature, and anisotropy exhibit distinct behavior near this point, which coincides with the place where the hopping frequency and this point overlap. Furthermore, our analysis includes the effect of pressure, showing that the Isotope Effect Coefficient and the critical temperature behave differently at this point under increasing pressure. We discussed how this phenomenon could be influenced by lattice defects, suggesting that H$_{3}$S could be subject to unconventional behavior under high-pressure conditions, possibly even exhibiting unconventional superconductivity characteristics. We explored this further, estimating an enhancement of the critical temperature by a factor of 20 when the van Hove singularity influences the Isotope Effect Coefficient, a more significant improvement than predicted by other theories. Conversely, our analysis also suggests a decrease of the critical temperature by almost two orders of magnitude when considering the anisotropy near this singularity. We have thus provided a more comprehensive understanding of the superconducting properties of the H$_{3}$S hydride, particularly the behavior of the Isotope Effect Coefficient as it relates to the van Hove singularity under high-pressure conditions. We hope this contributes to the search for superconducting materials and the broader impact of this discovery on the study of superconductivity at the molecular level. The results of this study can be used to develop a simple model to describe the behavior of superconducting materials, potentially opening doors for a new generation of superconducting technology, especially at high pressures. Robot motion planning typically becomes more complicated when obstacles are free to move. In this research, we focus on generating feasible paths for a single robot to navigate through dynamic environments where moving obstacles have specific goals and movement restrictions. A novel method, spatial restriction creation, is introduced to represent valid movement areas for obstacles in a global framework. By utilizing global constraint representations, efficient planning algorithms can be applied to both parallel and sequential computational frameworks. The key advantage of our approach lies in efficiently converting dynamic movement constraints into fixed spatial restrictions, which enables the use of existing global path planning algorithms. The efficacy of our proposed method is demonstrated through various simulations showcasing different types of movement constraints and goal locations. In experimental comparisons, we show that our method outperforms constraint-based techniques that rely solely on dynamic constraints. The method developed here has been successfully implemented on an Apple Siri Remote, enabling the planning of human-interactive robot motion in a responsive way. In system demonstrations, we successfully visualize and execute motion plans in a multi-device environment, showcasing the integration of our method with a motion planning pipeline. The proposed interface between spatial restriction creation and motion planning algorithms serves as a foundation for low-hardware, human-interactive robot planning systems. The method developed here has been successfully evaluated in various domains, including a simplified underwater search and rescue setting and a more complex robotic kitchen environment. In system comparisons, we successfully integrate our method with existing motion planning algorithms and high-level decision-making frameworks, demonstrating its potential to enhance robot safety through collaborative and productive interactions with humans. The existing research presents opportunities for further exploration and extension in various aspects of the domain, the constraint recognition process, and the evaluation of our method, which can lead to more general and flexible approaches to motion planning in diverse settings. The research presents an open challenge to the community to develop methods that can automatically derive spatial restriction creation from dynamic movement constraints, which could significantly enhance the automation of robot movement planning and execution. The research presents another open challenge to the community to integrate our method with advanced learning techniques that can automatically generate motion planning algorithms based on prior experience and long-term planning. The research presents an alternative solution to the community to integrate our method with more complex cognitive architectures that integrate robot movement planning with high-level decision-making frameworks. The integration of our method with a cognitive architecture requires a higher degree of robot movement planning automation. The research presents another alternative solution to the community to integrate our method with computationally efficient distributed motion planning algorithms, which can significantly enhance the scalability of our method in complex environments. The visual relocalization problem is being increasingly addressed by deep neural networks. However, these networks' dependence on large amounts of vast 2D training data restricts their application and consistency. A significant amount of manual labor is needed to create such training data, and transferring knowledge from one place to another is challenging due to shifts in lighting conditions. To overcome these challenges, utilizing 3D surfel mapping data derived from LiDAR sensors in autonomous driving and robotics offers a viable approach. Although incorporating LiDAR data complicates the process, it significantly enhances localization performance and consistency. To take advantage of 3D LiDAR data, we developed a novel framework for integrating map data and 2D images to boost the accuracy and dependability of visual relocalization. This framework uses a deep network to extract height-independent features from both map and live images, and then uses geometric information to build a spatial graph. Localization is then performed by determining a pose that optimally matches live image features with map features, based on the learned features' geometry and spatial relationships. Comprehensive experiments were conducted to assess the sensitivity of our method to different levels of map accuracy, and the results show that the proposed method achieves consistent and accurate results with both accurate and coarse maps, outperforming existing methods. Notably, when the map has 10% geometric error, the proposed method achieves a 2D localization accuracy of 2.80 meters, while a state-of-the-art 2D method fails to accurately localize even with a 5% map accuracy. This research explores the challenge of simultaneously encoding data and choosing users in a multiuser MIMO network, where multiple antennas transmit multiple signals to multiple users. To optimize performance, we aim to maximize the sum of users' data rates while keeping the transmitted signals simple. However, solving this problem directly is computationally complex, so we break it down into two interconnected tasks: selecting users and encoding. To achieve better results, we utilize Group LASSO's ability to select multiple users. An alternating algorithm is developed to solve each task, and its convergence is proven. Additionally, we relax the algorithm's constraints to improve encoding performance and reduce correlation between signals. Let L be a formal system that includes propositional logic, and let T be a tropical semifield. A set-valued function F can be viewed as a logical function semifield over T if its values satisfy certain conditions derived from formulas using elements and operations in T. A tropical curve comes equipped with a logical function semifield for the coordinate rings of its point sets, which can be viewed as subsemifields of T. This paper shows that the logical function semifields over T are generated by a finite collection involving point evaluation semifields and the tropical integer semifield, which is a subsemifield of any tropical function field over T. This achievement builds upon previous work similar semifields for tropical curves were investigated in Arav, Evans, and Neumann, while the definition and properties of the logical function semifields here were first introduced in Arav, Jekel, and Neumann. As a consequence of our research, the logical function semifields over the tropical plane are completely classified, providing evidence that the earlier developed classification of the logical function semifields over algebraic curves in another context is a broader, more general truth. Furthermore, the logical function semifields over T corresponding to rational resolvents of the tropical plane are also analyzed and understood in terms of tropical geometry, specifically through the birational model of the tropical plane and its associated linear subsemifields, which correspond to identity ideals in the tropical sense. It turns out that identity ideals in the tropical sense yield semifields that are dense in themselves, a property that was previously seen in the case of algebraic curves through the zero locus of a single polynomial. In the course of our research, the relationship between the logical function semifields over T and tropical geometry was investigated, revealing that the logical function semifields over T corresponding to rational resolvents of the tropical plane involve semi-algebraic sets with a particular algebraic expression related to the tropical coordinate variables and a single tropical polynomial. This relationship in the case of algebraic curves was through the zero locus of a single polynomial, while in the case of the tropical plane, a certain determinant must be nonnegative. The proof of this algebraic nature and the specified properties was approached through the combination of work by Dehning, Jekel, and Neumann on the density of the semifield of study and the work by Arav on the logical function semiffields over tropical curves, in addition to the application of tropical geometry results associated with Cartan, Elkin, and Minnelli that were previously unforeseen

It's demonstrated that the Vassiliev invariant of order three, linking number, can be calculated using a combination of the Fox-Hatcher loop and a one-sphere topological invariant. Although the Vassiliev invariant of order three is already well understood in terms of its component parts, this particular composition has not previously been discussed. The method employed here relies on a combination of the Fox-Hatcher loop, a one-sphere topological invariant, and the Kauffman bracket. By applying the Fox-Harter loop to a virtual link, it can calculate the Vassiliev invariant of order three, as well as the second and third cohomology groups of the braid group branched over the circle. As a side benefit, it is also shown that the Vassiliev invariant of order three, linking number, can serve as a one-sphere topological invariant. Furthermore, the Kauffman bracket is identified as a composition of three cohomology groups for the braid group branched over the circle. The article provides explicit calculations for the coefficients involved. Calculations for the second and third cohomology groups of the braid group branched over the circle are also presented. This proposed transition is analogous to a similar process in QCD, where the theory progresses through different stages, analogous to the phases of baryon formation. Additionally, we use a gauge invariant, short-range potential to better comprehend the theory's low-energy properties. Thorough examinations of the theory's static balance equations at distinct points along this transition process confirm that it successfully propagates through distinct phases, maintaining stability and robust anomaly characteristics, consistent with both the chiral effective theory prediction and the standard model, while also replicating color SU(N) features. Furthermore, this theory's chiral gauge invariant, short-range potential emerges at the quark condensation end of the transition, mirroring characteristics of four-dimensional QCD. This work sheds new light on a well-known theoretical model, the four-dimensional Curtis-Pennington model, helping to clarify its behavior and significance. This research introduces dual alterations for Loidreau's code-based cryptography system. 

Originally, Loidreau's system operates with a secret matrix $G_0$ and public matrix $G_1$ formed by stacked generator matrices of a cyclic code, with $G_0$ containing the fundamental vectors and $G_1$ composed of the secondary vectors. 

We present two public-key alteration methods: 

 1. The first method replaces a portion of $G_0$'s rows with $G_1$ rows, keeping the intersection of orthonormal vectors, which remains secure and doesn't impact the code's dimension.
 2. The second method involves substituting a subset of $G_0$ and $G_1$ rows within parity-check equations, with specific parity-check matrices, which provides an advantageous system performance in terms of complexity and size. 

Both alterations ensure the parity-check matrix has the same rank as the original and remain secure since the shared and unique vectors can't be distinguished from one another. 
In the case of a random cyclic code, this translates to shared and unique vectors having random weights. 
In the case of a cyclic code derived from a primitive polynomial, this indicates a bias in the weights of the shared and unique vectors, which can be measured using a weight distribution bias metric. 
The application of the second alteration is demonstrated with a few specific cyclic codes and various weights for $G_0$ and $G_1$, which shows improved system performance when bias is minimized. 
The system performance is evaluated in terms of the complexity of the matrix product $PG_0^TX_0$ and size of the matrix product $PG_1^TX_1$, where $P$ and $X_0, X_1$ are the parity-check and code matrices. 
The altered system has been shown to offer increased security against the XL algorithm. 
The security analysis was carried out for a range of weights using the weight distribution bias metric, 
The system's performance was evaluated for 16, 17 and 19-bit weights for both alterations. 
The results showed that as the weight distribution bias metric increased, the system performance also increased. 
We observed that alteration 1 showed similar performance to the original system when the weight distribution bias metric was less than 0.05. 
Alteration 2 showed similar performance to the original system when the bias metric was less than 0.2.

Existing research has effectively addressed the privacy concerns associated with deciding whether data can be used to train machine learning models, but the issue of data diffusion remains unexplored. I introduce the concept of data diffusion, characterized by the release of intermediate information that aids future model development without compromising existing ones. While data diffusion introduces complications, as the released information may conflict with previous results, it also presents an opportunity to enhance the overall efficiency of machine learning model development. I have developed two key contributions: first, algorithms for privately learning decision trees on distributed data, and second, a precise calculation of data diffusion's impact on model learning accuracy. I have also devised an expandable algorithm to handle the challenges posed by data diffusion. The effectiveness of my methods was confirmed through experiments involving synthetic data, and the results were compared to existing approaches in decision tree learning, particularly those utilizing the SVM algorithm with a privacy protection framework known as Baggart. Analysis revealed that data diffusion may either enhance or diminish the overall efficiency of model learning, contingent upon the type of algorithms employed and the amount of data diffusion that occurs. Given a certain level of data diffusion, the algorithms performed significantly better at higher diffusion levels, indicating that data diffusion can enhance efficiency. However, excessive data diffusion may also occur when algorithms perform poorly, indicating a potential trade-off in efficiency and data diffusion efficiency. I propose multiple future research avenues. Firstly, investigating specific data diffusion effects on models trained with certain algorithms. Secondly, developing a precision optimization algorithm to balance efficiency and accuracy when dealing with data diffusion. Thirdly, studying the long-term effects of data diffusion, and whether it can lead to overfitting or the development of weak models. Fourthly, establishing a standard method to measure data diffusion effects. Fifthly, developing methods to cause data diffusion for certain algorithms. Sixthly, using data diffusion to solve other complex problems, such as data privacy concerns. We compare various formulations of beta-divergence, consider alternative methods for their parameters, and discuss links between our approach and existing techniques, particularly minimization-based methods for the Kullback-Leibler beta-divergence. We examine numerical performance in image denoising applications, comparing different cost functions and priors under realistic conditions. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively denoise synthetic and real-world images, even when the R\'enyi alpha parameter is high or low, and that the choice of cost function significantly affects the denoising outcome. Furthermore, the paper highlights the importance of prior information in the denoising process and demonstrates that the proposed method can handle any type of beta-divergence, including the log-contrastive divergence with no additional parameters required. This research generalizes existing methods to handle a broader class of divergences while providing a unified framework for performing divergence minimization. We also provide an open-source implementation of the method to facilitate its application. Additionally, the paper examines the logarithmic Laplace and log-explicit R\'enyi divergences, considering the potential advantages of these alternatives over the standard Kullback-Leibler and squared difference divergences in various applications. In practice, the logarithmic Laplace divergence performs similarly to the standard Kullback-Leibler divergence but offers a more balanced trade-off between the Kullback-Leibler and squared difference divergences. Conversely, the log-explicit R\'enyi alpha=0 divergence performs closer to the log-Kullback-Leibler divergence than the standard Kullback-Leibler divergence, although the log-explicit R\'enyi alpha=0 and squared distance divergences exhibit similar outcomes at the level of the probability estimates, with the log-explicit R\'enyi alpha=0 preserving more information about the underlying true distribution. Consequently, the logarithmic Laplace divergence is suggested as the preferred choice for applications requiring a balanced trade-off, while the log-explicit R\'enyi alpha=0 divergence is recommended for applications prioritizing accuracy. This paper presents a novel Bayesian framework for choosing the optimal chain event network (CEN) model among multiple options by evaluating their respective MAP models. The proposed framework calculates the Bayesian posterior probability of each model based on the likelihood and prior probabilities. The models' likelihoods are estimated using the data's log-likelihood under the maximal a posteriori (MAP) parameter conditions, while their prior probabilities are determined based on their complexity and the number of generated models. This approach empowers the Bayesian framework to select CEN models by combining network structure and parameter evaluation, and to assess model uncertainty. Furthermore, the Bayesian framework is shown to outperform other model selection approaches, such as the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), on various synthetic networks. The method is applied to two case studies: the Ebola outbreak in Sierra Leone and the FX trading CEN models. The results confirm the effectiveness of the Bayesian framework in selecting suitable CEN models. These Euler-Lagrange equations encompass a broad range of curvature functionals, including the crystalline curvature itself, developed by the first author and Jerison, as part of a broader class of extrinsic curvature flows that have been studied in the mathematics community over the past few years. This movement is similar to crystalline curvature flow, which is always extrinsically regular, despite being a first-order flow with inherent complexities. This paper explores the current progress in this area, including the integration of an ancillary harmonic map, which facilitates the regularity analysis for this class of flows. It outlines the current results for this movement, including existence results for one-dimensional regular graphs and curves with bounded variation, as well as existence and long-term behavior for X-Lagrangean curvature flows. Additionally, this paper discusses several open questions that remain to be addressed. Ultimately, this movement is expected to be a topic of ongoing research in geometric PDEs. Human-written headlines are a vital component of news, enabling readers to quickly determine whether a story is significant or irrelevant. However, machine-devised headlines often fall short, rendering them untrustworthy. Current methods for evaluating headline authenticity rely on manual assessment and lack support from large, fine-grained datasets. In this research, we employ a neural network model, specifically the BERT series of transformers, to classify the origin of professionally crafted headlines. The presence of discrete time translation symmetry in quantum matter is a crucial factor that determines its physical properties. When dealiasing this symmetry by temperature or disorder, quantum matter shifts towards a critical state characterized by increased fluctuations. Our study demonstrates the importance of breaking this symmetry by topological defects to trigger this critical shift. We maintain the continuity between ordered and disordered phases, avoiding the dichotomy between crystals and liquids. Instead, we adopt a broad framework incorporating amorphous and polycrystalline phases to describe this critical shift. Utilizing this framework, we reevaluate well-known examples, such as chiral Weyl semimetal and chiral topological insulator phase transitions, and show that they can be subsumed within a broader phase diagram. Our approach is based on a new understanding of disorder and symmetry-broken phases, deviating from traditional crystal vs. liquid dichotomies. By viewing symmetry and its dealiasing mechanisms through a defect-defect network, we are able to uncover a rich complex of phases and describe their critical shifts. Furthermore, we propose that these shifts could be directly observed using scanning tunneling spectroscopy, especially when mediated by spin-incoherent tunneling processes. Our findings provide a general framework for understanding critical shifts and identify novel pathways to chiral spin liquids. They also have significant implications for theory and simulation, suggesting that ordered phases with topological defects are more stable than their disordered counterparts, and that crystal and amorphous phases are distinct from each other. Finally, they open up new avenues for experimental investigation into these phases and their potential realization in new materials. Ultimately, the majority of sources estimated by both conventional and adaptive Bayesian neural networks exhibit statistical significance above the confidence level employed in the extragalactic catalog. Individuals with disabilities are increasingly interacting with social media, which is transforming the way content is created and consumed. Building on the success of accessibility initiatives in web and mobile application development, our study delves into the practices of creating accessible content on social media platforms. Focusing on visual content creation, which is crucial for consumers with visual impairments, our research reveals the obstacles faced by content creators attempting to provide accessibilities such as captions and descriptions on Instagram and Twitter. Five key challenges were identified through interviews with seven experts: the lack of awareness and difficulties surrounding accessibility implementation, the impact of content creation workflows and limitations, the minimal feedback for content creators, the perception of accessibility as an added expense rather than an opportunity, and the dynamic nature of social media platform policies and technologies. Our findings offer a comprehensive understanding of accessible content creation on social media, which can serve as a foundation for future research and guide developers and content creators in providing better accessibilities for consumers with disabilities. Ultimately, our study explores strategies to make accessible content creation a more sustainable option for providers and encourages social media platforms to prioritize accessibility as a competitive advantage rather than a hurdle. In this paper, we introduce a novel hypergraph property known as the tensor union, which is derived from the Boolean tensor product. A counterpart to the notion of the union of sets, the tensor union of hypergraphs A1,..., Am has a certain similarity, but rather than relying on set inclusion, it uses the Boolean tensor product to combine the hypergraphs. We establish A1,..., Am to have non-zero tensor union if and only if a specific condition is met and present several applications involving this property. Moreover, we identify the integral spectrum characteristics of the tensor union and demonstrate its connection to the Euler characteristic. Specifically, for n = 1, the tensor union yields the conventional set union and its spectrum matches the integral spectrum of the symmetric coordinate rank function. Additionally, for |A| = 1 hypergraphs, the tensor union's spectrum aligns with the elementary dichotomy rank function. The spectrum's characteristics also answer an open query in reference [Hypergraph Spectra and Contagion, 2020]. The introduced hypergraph property finds its application in reference [Tensor Products and Boolean Hypergraph Properties, 2022] when analyzing the tensor product of hypergraphs. The presented research also points out a crucial requirement for hypergraph property preservation under the Boolean tensor product. Furthermore, we present several examples to illustrate the introduced concepts and their differences with the symmetric and elementary rank functions. The research is implemented using the AlgebrasOfClones package in the SwanneeC library. Lastly, we present several open questions related to the further exploration of the tensor union and Boolean tensor product in hypergraph theory.
