In a future 14 TeV LHC study, the production of $\phi$ in $t\overline{t}\phi$ processes will be analyzed to determine the Higgs boson's coupling to fermions. This analysis will involve a simplified model where a singlet scalar, $\phi$, couples only to fermions. Two distinct production modes, hadronically detected $t\overline{t}\phi$, will be examined to derive the Higgs boson's Yukawa coupling in relation to its mass. This investigation will have a significant role in understanding Yukawa coupling behavior, especially if its value is found to be different from unitarity limits, indicating new physics beyond the Standard Model. On the other hand, the measurement of the Higgs boson's Yukawa coupling itself will be more challenging, especially for its lower-mass region due to increased background competition. Consequently, the focus of this study will be on the dataset of $\sim$300 ${\rm fb}^{-1}$, where Higgs-yukawa is most sensitive to new physics. Furthermore, the inclusion of leptonic $t\overline{t}\phi$ detection, although influenced by increased backgrounds, will provide additional detection possibilities, particularly for its leptonic component with leptons. The study, based on the latest DELPHI's CMS detector simulation, has shown that the $t\overline{t}\phi$ production in its hadronic and leptonic modes can be detected with statistical significance at $3\,\sigma$ and $5\,\sigma$ confidence level for $\phi$ masses below $140\,{\rm GeV}$ and integrated luminosities of $300\,{\rm fb}^{-1}$ and $300\,{\rm fb}^{-1}$ and $1\,{\rm fb}^{-1}$ respectively. The hadronic detection, although providing best statistical accuracy for $\log_{10}({\rm Yuk})$ and its derivative, is found to be limited by theoretical uncertainties in its global fit for $\log_{10}({\rm Yuk})$. On the other hand, the measurement is found to be less dependent on these uncertainties when determined from its leptonic detection at significantly increased statistical precision for specific $\phi$ mass points. The study has shown that the $t\overline{t}\phi$ production in its hadronic and leptonic modes can be effectively used to test the Higgs-yukawa behavior under Standard Model and new-fermionic coupling behaviors.

The process of converting computer text into a uniform format is known as text standardization. This process can be difficult due to variations in language formats. One method of improving text standardization involves using data normalization during the training of a model. This process, known as inverse text standardization, improves model training by normalizing the training data. Despite its effectiveness, this method is often complicated and may not be suitable for uncommon formats. To overcome these limitations, we investigated combining data normalization with other text standardization techniques. Our research involved applying data enhancement methods to a text standardization dataset to increase its size and diversity. This allowed us to evaluate the impact of varying dataset properties on a text standardization model's performance. Our experiments showed that certain dataset properties could significantly affect a model's performance, and that adjusting these properties through data enhancement could improve a model's results. Ultimately, our integrated approach of combining data normalization with data enhancement achieved better results than either method used separately. Transformers' success in areas like natural language translation and image processing has made its variants the preferred choice for many state-of-the-art architectures. A crucial factor behind this success is the multi-head attention mechanism in Transformers, which is renowned for its capacity to model complex interactions across input and output spaces. Although attention mechanisms typically require inputs of the same size, a subset known as 'Tangent' handles inputs of arbitrary size by transforming them, thus enabling the creation of scalable architectures. A notable issue with these 'Tangent' approaches, however, is the need to train separate models for different input sizes, which can lead to a substantial number of models to train and maintain. To address this challenge, we present NFT-K, a universal image transformer that size-transposes input tensors, thereby allowing a single model to handle various input sizes without compromising performance. A pivotal role in NFT-K's design is the use of Non-Exchangeable Tangent (NET) transformations, which can reconfigure a transformer's input tensor into a different shape while maintaining the tensor's underlying structure. By integrating multiple, sequentially applied NETs, NFT-K is able to size-transpose input tensors to arbitrary dimensions. Through experiments conducted on ImageNet-1K using a single model that can handle different input sizes, NFT-K has achieved state-of-the-art results, specifically an accuracy of 86.8% for an input size of 1280 and an accuracy of 84.2% for an input size of 512. Additionally, NFT-K's code is publicly available at the repository link. Research has been conducted under the grant number GUGA20294/2021. With the rise of Artificial Intelligence on Internet of Things devices, these systems rely heavily on machine learning for efficient communication with users between devices and humans. This interface necessitates a method for selecting key phrases from lengthy text based on a device's status, which a user can subsequently view on their screen. Although machine learning methods have been widely applied and successfully implemented in various areas of IoT, their use in choosing key phrases has been largely neglected. A novel approach using Neural Networks for Key Phrase Detection on IoT has been lacking in research, an area we aim to address. This study evaluates and compares three key network architecture choices, specifically Convolutional Networks, Recurrent Networks, and Transformer Networks, by considering factors like memory requirements, processing speed, and adaptability to status descriptions of differing lengths. Our analysis involves an extensive analysis of the challenges and limitations associated with choosing key phrases on IoT devices, an area of research that has been largely overlooked in existing literature. The proposed framework was then evaluated on publicly available datasets, with the results suggesting that a suitable choice of network architecture depends largely on the dataset being used. Ultimately, our analysis points to a new research path that requires careful consideration of a dataset's characteristics. This insight is crucial in addressing the unique requirements and challenges associated with choosing key phrases on IoT devices and the specific network architecture choice that should be employed. Based on our analysis, a Convolutional Network appears to be the most suitable option given its relatively small memory requirements and swift processing speed, making it well-suited for choosing key phrases on devices with limited storage capacity and a fast data processing system. Nonetheless, there are scenarios where a dataset exhibits notable changes in length, in which case a Recurrent Network or a Transformer Network may be a more suitable choice. Overall, our analysis provides a valuable starting point for researchers and practitioners looking to develop effective key phrase detection solutions on IoT devices. Deep learning-based controllers are widely employed in various complex systems, such as self-driving cars and robotic arms, due to their ability to process high-dimensional data, like images and sensor readings, and adapt to dynamic environments. Notably, they can also be used to introduce controller failures as a cyber threat to other systems. Because of this, there's a pressing need to develop methods for detecting and mitigating compromised controllers. Unfortunately, it's very hard to teach a controller to be resilient to attacks by providing detailed information about the threat as the threat can be unknown or can change. Because of the difficulty and cost associated with testing on physical systems, model-driven approaches are often preferred for developing controllers. We propose a new model-driven method called Resilience Through Model Exploitation (RME) that can enhance the resilience of a controller to malicious inputs without the need for detailed information on the attack. Our method uses a deep reinforcement learning approach to automatically discover the controller's resilience by balancing the exploration and exploitation of model-generated inputs within a simulation environment. We test our method on a simulated car system subject to cyber attacks and compare it with other approaches. The concept of geometric scaling will be explored in relation to QCD and its various regimes of saturation. Initially, the connection between geometric scaling and conformal scaling will be established, before demonstrating its occurrence in various scenarios such as gluon distributions within protons, initial conditions for gluon rapidity distributions in large nuclei, and even momenta. It will also be shown that geometric scaling can be observed in various combinations, such as in collisions involving heavy nuclei. To achieve this, we will review the principles of a non-linear QCD model known as the CKS model. Furthermore, we will discuss how geometric scaling can serve as an effective tool for determining the saturation momentum $Q_s$ in various contexts. Finally, we will explore potential relationships between geometric scaling and observables that remain unaltered by collisions, such as the 'blackness' of nuclei and a specific quantity associated with the 'dielectric constant' in a non-linear QCD medium, known as the 'dielectric constant observable' or $\cal{O}$($F_{\rm dielectric}$). As the 'dielectric constant observable' is known to exhibit geometric scaling, it can be utilized to predict the occurrence of geometric scaling for an infinite nucleus, even before a saturation momentum is attained. Additionally, we will discuss possible collisions that may lead to a situation where an infinite 'dielectric constant observable' is observed. In such cases, we will demonstrate that geometric scaling occurs automatically and predict that it should also occur during collisions involving a large enough impact parameter. Ultimately, we will explore the possibility that the 'dielectric constant observable' may serve as an effective pre-conditions criterion for observing geometric scaling in various contexts. Various simulations will be presented to illustrate these concepts. Lastly, some of the corresponding numerical results from other approaches will be compared to those simulated within this context. Relevant discussions on potential relationships between geometric scaling and observables that remain unaltered by collisions, such as the 'blackness' of nuclei and the 'dielectric constant observable' or $\cal{O}$($F_{\rm dielectric}$), will also be included. In particular, similar work from other approaches will be discussed, including a recent corresponding letter and a related presentation at the 'Workshop on Geometric Scaling in QCD' held at the University of California, Santa Barbara. The interplay of electron interaction and band structure anisotropies plays a crucial role in the electrical properties of bilayer graphene. When interactions across different layers are limited, we demonstrate that the renormalization group flow reveals an approach that balances interaction enhancement within each layer with a collapse of the other-layer tunning parameter to zero. In this scenario, we establish two instability scales: one related to fractional Hall states and another to an interacting fermion bag phase initially proposed for 3D systems. Furthermore, if both in-layer and inter-layer interactions are long-range, we show that his layer's kinetic energy is completely renormalized to zero, leading to a state with flat bands. We also investigate the effects of long-range interactions on the band structure and compute the scaling dimension responsible for the related instability using the renormalization group flow method. In addition, we discuss how properties of a 2D fermion gas at low density, where Landau parameters are dominant, can be applied to bilayer graphene through a Landau parameter renormalization approach. The relationship between these parameters provides a method to map 2D models onto bilayer graphene and reverse the process, mapping bilayer graphene to a 2d system. The model for the 2d system features a nontrivial, fractionalized effective magnetic field, which arises due to the coupling to a chiral 2d system. A novel, flexible sample size reassessment strategy for Bayesian clinical trials is proposed and suited for adaptive trials in Ramsey-type studies. In contrast to traditional frequency domain auditory testing using critical threshold assessment, we utilize auditory orientation tasks that provide direct threshold assessment in time domain. We create a Bayesian predictive model for auditory threshold distribution, which yields high accuracy despite fewer measurements than traditional approaches. A simulation study confirms that our approach can determine the optimal sample size with fewer participants, while maintaining sufficient data for a well-informed go/no-go decision after trial reevaluation. A participant safety mechanism is also implemented, allowing the trial to be terminated early if new information indicates a lack of treatment effect. A real-world application is further detailed, involving auditory orientation tasks in the frequency domain, which validates the effectiveness of our sample size reassessment strategy. A related R package, bayrsv2, facilitates the implementation of this approach in actual trials.

A new quantum Monte Carlo method has been proposed that efficiently uses qubits and dynamic quantum optimization techniques to tackle challenging many-body problems in quantum chemistry. Unlike traditional N-qubit approaches that are hindered by excessive excitation states, this method adapts and reduces the number of qubits as the simulation progresses, keeping the qubit error margin within a predetermined threshold. Each step involves a quantum quantum optimization algorithm that moves the system towards a lower energy state. To validate its efficacy, the adaptive solver was applied to the Be and H$_2$ molecules at various intermolecular distances. When compared to the full quantum Hilbert space calculations, the results show that the adaptive solver outperforms traditional N-qubit methods while also competing with even lower N-qubit methods that require more complicated state mappings. Notably, the method exhibits robustness in the presence of weak interactions and accurately reproduces energetic transitions between states. These findings indicate that the adaptive solver has the potential to efficiently handle simulations of arbitrary accuracy and may be used to study excited states and energetic transitions in large molecules. Further research is needed to expand the method to simulate interactions between light and heavy particles. The source code for this method has been made available.

In recent years, generative models have gained significant attention due to their capability to produce high-quality samples and approximate intricate distributions. Conversely, inverse models have received less focus, despite their potential to uncover the underlying causes behind data samples. By assuming that data samples originate from latent representations, inverse models can play a crucial role in both unsupervised representation learning and manipulation tasks. Notably, a thorough examination of the reverse transformation itself can lead to further understanding of the data representations. However, most techniques are incapable of accurately addressing this problem, primarily due to the non-smooth and non-differentiable nature of discrete representation vectors. To address this limitation, a method known as the Profound Neural Landscapes framework is proposed, employing a differentiable and approximated inverse mapping that both constrains and differentiates the representations. This approach is capable of leveraging the strengths of both neural networks (in the form of a generative model) and variational inference, thus providing a unified framework for the simultaneous learning of generative and inverse models. The proposed method, known as the Generative Decoder Profound (GDP), is capable of utilizing a generative model as a means of approximating the reverse transformation while also gaining profound insights into the structure of the representations. Furthermore, GDP is capable of leveraging the reconstruction error and phase estimation loss introduced by Profound, thus enhancing the quality of the generated samples and the coherence of the manipulated images. Evaluating the optimal balance between high precision and excessive background noise from inflationary gravitational waves is a critical challenge for next-generation cosmological observations.  NANOGrav's recent findings of a possible signal indicate an optimal frequency range for sensitivity and compatibility with other cosmological constraints.  Analyzing this range in the context of a robust signal amplification mechanism from inflation, we find that the observed NANOGrav amplitude can be generated with minimal deviation from the standard cosmological model.  Specifically, we find that the radiation-dominated k-index can account for the observed amplitude at a frequency three times lower than NANOGrav's peak sensitivity, with minimal impact on cosmological parameters.  Conversely, the robust signal mechanism requires a k-index significantly lower than one, which can be inconsistent with other cosmological constraints such as Planck's large-scale structure observations.  In agreement with recent LIGO-Virgo findings, our analysis suggests that the optimal parameter range for cosmological consistency may be outside the amplitude range that would be optimal for detecting a pure inflationary gravitational wave background.  Therefore, to design experiments that would be optimal for detecting a pure background, these should commence when the noise floor is still higher than the amplitude, with the understanding that the difference between the noiseless and the actual optimal amplitude remains within the range that would be detectable with a pure background.  By combining data from NANOGrav, Planck, and other cosmological observations, our analysis suggests that the optimal parameter range for cosmological consistency includes a k-index around 0.2 and 0.3, which can also explain the amplitude of the NANOGrav's possible signal at its peak frequency with the understanding that the optimal parameter range for noiseless conditions would be lower than 0.2.  Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the optimal parameter range for cosmological consistency could also be achieved with the presence of a red tilt in the primordial tensor power spectrum, which could also explain the amplitude of the NANOGrav's possible signal at its peak frequency with the understanding that the optimal parameter range for noiseless conditions would be lower than 0.2.  In a different scenario where the noiseless conditions are higher than 0.2, our analysis suggests that the red tilt in the primordial tensor power spectrum can also explain the amplitude of the NANOGrav's possible signal at its peak frequency with the understanding that the optimal parameter range for cosmological consistency could also be achieved with the presence of a k-index around 0.

During its 2016 closest approach to the Sun, the comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS), with a highly eccentric orbit, provided an exceptional opportunity for scientific investigation. A unique aspect of this comet was its presence in the interplanetary region between Mars and Jupiter, where it was studied using molecular line observations collected by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). Operating under less-than-ideal observational circumstances due to the comet's small size and distant position from Mars, a dedicated effort was made to assess its performance by comparing it with previous observations of more favorable comets. By examining six spectral lines, including CO, CS, CN, C2H5CN, H2CO, and H2CS, the results indicated a comet significantly less active than those encountered by deep space missions such as Comet 67P/Chayim El Nino but more active than comets visited by the flyby mission 1I/2018 UG. A notable discovery was the detection of carbon monosulfide in comets for the very first time. To gain insight into the possible production mechanisms of CS, a variety of models were applied to the comet's gas and molecular compositions, revealing a compelling case for CS to originate from grains. A potential explanation for this origin includes the sulfides and sulfites formed through the interaction of sulfur compounds with water and oxygen within the interstellar medium. It is suggested that future investigations into the presence of sulfur compounds in comets could further illuminate this phenomenon. The availability of vast speech data makes unsupervised speech generation using transformer models appealing, given its ability to handle large unlabelled speech datasets efficiently. Despite the model's potential, current approaches often run into issues such as speech-quality degradation during unsupervised learning or require time-consuming sampling processes. To tackle these problems, we present an unsupervised speech generation approach that relies on a straightforward, efficient, and easy-to-implement latent variable model. Unsupervised learning is achieved by adding noise to existing speech samples, effectively creating pseudo-targets. Notably, our method boasts a reduced O(1) sampling complexity, significantly outperforming existing solutions. Experimental evaluations across several domains confirm the efficacy of our approach in producing high-quality speech samples in less time compared to state-of-the-art methods. To facilitate further research, our method, implementation, and pre-trained models are made publicly available. Our results indicate a significant quality improvement (9.38-19.58% relative) over state-of-the-art methods in various speech generation tasks. Moreover, the unsupervised learning phase yields speech samples with a higher F1 score (11.16-42.16% relative) and lower sampling complexity (98.7% less or several orders of magnitude more efficient). To supplement these findings, acoustic metrics, the impact of hyperparameters, and the effect of model architecture on the unsupervised speech generation task are also examined. The core of aspect-based sentiment analysis lies in uncovering the ambiguous sentiment patterns linking aspects to emotions and words to meanings. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel pre-training technique that focuses on the contrastive representation of ambiguous sentiments, which enhances the sentiment representations by highlighting their internal contradictions and external connections. By incorporating guided regularization, this method aims to improve the sentiment representations by constraining similar sentiments towards unification and dissimilar sentiments towards differentiation. To further improve performance, we develop a refined fine-tuning framework with a guided contrastive loss and a sentiment-guided aspect-aspect similarity model. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through extensive experiments on six publicly available datasets, surpassing current state-of-the-art models in all datasets in the aspect-emotion classification task and rivaling the best performance in the aspect-based sentiment analysis task when compared to other available methods. This study addresses the challenge of evaluating the presence of mediators in binary mediation models when dealing with selected case-control data. A novel score-based approach is proposed that allows for assessing presence or absence of mediators through various distributional assumptions about mediators. Furthermore, an asymptotic theory is developed for score statistics in binary mediation models, revealing that these scores can be interpreted as test statistics to evaluate indirect effects, mediation ratios, and probability of mediation. These score statistics also admit equivalent parametric tests. Additionally, it is demonstrated that using logistic regression for selected case-control data can lead to statistically significant results for indirect effects, mediation ratios, and probability of mediation even if the null hypothesis is true, under specific data generation mechanisms. However, it is observed that using logistic regression for selected case-control data does not affect the test statistics for indirect effects, mediation ratios, and probability of mediation obtained using score-based methods under non-informative data generation mechanisms. Lastly, a simulation study is conducted to compare the performance of score-based methods, logistic regression, and confidence interval methods. Observations from the simulation study indicate that when the null hypothesis is true, score-based methods using non-informative data generation mechanisms yield fewer type I errors than logistic regression for selected case-control data, especially for smaller effect sizes. Additionally, score-based methods appear to exhibit greater power for larger effect sizes. However, score-based methods may experience reduced power for smaller effect sizes due to conservatively controlling the type I error rate. Confidence interval methods using non-informative data generation mechanisms also result in slightly narrower intervals but fail to control the type I error rate in some scenarios. Observations from the simulation study also suggest that using non-informative data generation mechanisms during the analysis may lead to more reliable and interpretable results, albeit with reduced power. A real-data example is provided to illustrate the effectiveness of score-based methods for evaluating presence or absence of mediators in binary mediation models when dealing with selected case-control data. A companion paper focuses on evaluating the strength of mediators in binary mediation models when dealing with selected case-control data. The Unruh effect, which describes the transformation of vacuum into a thermal state in the presence of a uniformly accelerating observer, has been experimentally replicated using quantum optics. Classical fields in an accelerating frame behave quantumly, and this phenomenon can be observed both theoretically and experimentally. A new approach has been formulated to quantify the entanglement between past and future light cones in non-inertial frames. This phase, which occurs when the acceleration changes, correlates with a geometric effect found in certain quantum systems possessing a fundamental geometric structure. Experimentally, we have demonstrated that the entanglement within the light cones can be detected across various accelerations. Additionally, we have found that the entanglement between past and future light cones is not necessarily present in stationary frames, even if the trajectories form a closed loop in space-time. On the other hand, the entanglement does arise across the spacelike interval connecting the past and future, and this phenomenon is, in fact, equivalent to the temporal Berry phase associated with the entanglement of spacelike separated events. An alternative method has also been formulated to measure the temporal Berry phase, which does not rely on accelerating frames. Furthermore, we have established that the temporal Berry phase is an efficient indicator of the Unruh effect and can be applied to a wide range of quantum systems. Finally, we have derived a connection between the temporal Berry phase and the vacuum noise that accelerators produce, revealing that the latter can be calculated based on the former. An associated device, which delves into the fundamental properties of quantum systems, has also been presented in this framework. This research explores the possibility of quantitatively measuring quantum-geometric effects in non-accelerating systems using local observables, thereby enabling the detection of Unruh effect with significantly enhanced precision. Such geometric effects may serve as a means to detect the Unruh effect in systems lacking accelerating observers, thereby replicating the effect at a more simplified level. An accompanying experiment has also been described, which has successfully measured the temporal Berry phase under various acceleration levels and has also demonstrated its application in detecting the Unruh effect in both accelerating and non-accelerating systems. Importantly, we have experimentally verified that the temporal Berry phase is an efficient indicator of the Unruh effect in systems lacking accelerating observers. An accompanying quantum optics experiment has also been presented, which has replicated the Unruh effect in a quantum optical setup and has demonstrated the application of the temporal Berry phase as an efficient indicator of the Unruh effect in an experimental context.

To understand everyday life situations, it's crucial to identify the occasion or social context behind events. Recognizing occasions is vital for making informed decisions, both personally and professionally. Until now, available data sources have significant limitations, primarily due to a lack of multilingual coverage and comprehensive occasion definitions. To address these challenges, we have created the Multilingual Occasion Extraction Dataset, which is unique in several ways. First, it covers three diverse languages: English, Spanish, and Hindi. Second, it encompasses 2,000 occasion entities, with 1,000 from each language, across 200 distinct categories. Third, each entry in MEE has three definitions, along with three event phrases to test occasion extraction. Finally, 1,800 question-answer pairs in each language are included to facilitate question answering based on the identified occasions. Our experiments using MEE demonstrate that the dataset is effective in evaluating multilingual models' capabilities, especially in occasion extraction and related tasks. Notably, the dataset and accompanying evaluation code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/allenai/MEE-Dataset. Moreover, our results from various benchmarking datasets using cutting-edge multilingual pre-trained language models reveal substantial room for improvement in multilingual occasion extraction. Specifically, the top-performing model, ALBERT-2, achieves an F1-score of 66.1% (English), 65.5% (Spanish), and 58.1% (Hindi) in the MEE dataset. A similar assessment using the TimeBank dataset (English) indicates an F1-score of 66.1%. These results underscore the need for improved techniques in multilingual occasion extraction and related tasks. Finally, the potential applications of MEE are not limited to occasion extraction; the dataset can also facilitate a range of other natural language processing tasks, including knowledge representation, question answering, text generation, and related tasks. To further enhance these applications, we plan to develop approaches for generating text based on occasions and related entities. Specifically, the winning model in the related QA challenge, MSALoRA, achieves an F1-score and EM-score of 85.4% and 70.1% respectively. Consequently, the next goal is to improve these scores, ultimately making the occasion or social context behind events more explicit in language. We introduce an altered RingCT protocol that facilitates anonymous transactions for Bitcoin and other forked cryptocurrencies. Our improved method relies on Clinger, a lightweight verifiable delay function, to expedite the mixing process within the MixCoins service. These integrated MixCoins and Delegated RingCT constitute a delegated mixing system. Delegated RingCT incorporates Delegated Ring Signatures (DRS), leveraging public key cryptography mechanisms for the signing and verification process, thus allowing participants to remain unidentified. Additionally, DRS enhances RingCT's transactional anonymity by incorporating sender and recipient identifiers into each transaction. Our implementation of DRS within the Bitcoin protocol necessitates a new opcode, and we examine various security aspects related to unlinkability and untraceability, impersonation, and key generation, as well as compute and storage demands. Furthermore, we simulate MixCoins services powered by Clinger and assess their performance based on different parameters, ultimately concluding that Delegated RingCT can decrease RingCT transaction creation time by approximately two-fold. Given its anonymity features and reduced computational requirements, our solution can effectively safeguard users within Bitcoin-like cryptocurrencies. The proposed approach leverages quadrature techniques applied to isotropic and anisotropic solar models, ultimately leading to simplified formulas for calculating solar irradiance through Gaussian quadrature. The resulting method precisely simulates the standard solar spectrum defined by AM0, enabling the transformation of solar signals into their corresponding photoelectric currents and heat inputs. The quadrature method's computational simplicity and non-iterative nature make it a versatile tool applicable to various solar-energy simulations and analyses. Calculating this for all parameters would require computing and storing a massive second-order matrix, which previous methods attempted to circumvent but became inefficient and unstable. New techniques, such as viiT, have successfully recovered second derivative information for a neural network from its Jacobian matrix, leveraging the generalized Gauss-Newton's low-dimensional structure. By leveraging the generalized Gauss-Newton's collapsed Hessian, viiT achieves this in a computationally efficient manner, enabling accurate curvature-based optimization techniques and stable training, and we demonstrate its potential on various tasks. As a result, viiT's efficient and stable tools promote an emphasis on accurate second derivative information for neural networks, and we anticipate their broad application in future research. In languages that specify grammatical gender, common nouns are assigned a fixed gender without regard to the actual entities they represent. This implicit link between nouns and gender could potentially affect how humans and machines understand noun meanings. To explore this connection, we analyzed how grammatical gender affects the semantic interpretation of nouns using large-scale distributional word vectors. Our results indicate that grammatical gender has a noticeable impact on how we interpret nouns. Furthermore, we discovered links between a word's etymology and the gender assigned to related words, providing etymological context can help clarify these interpretations. Since gender assignment criteria vary significantly across languages, we conclude that taking grammatical gender into consideration is particularly essential in contexts where it influences language usage, such as in information retrieval or text classification tasks. Our proposed approach could aid in uncovering the explicit connections between grammatical gender and noun meanings, thereby enhancing gender prediction models for under-resourced languages. Ultimately, we suggest that incorporating grammatical gender into distributional semantic models can improve their effectiveness in understanding words in context. This suggested improvement warrants further exploration in future research. 

The findings presented here are based on experiments conducted with 11 languages, and the associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/melodiepoole/grammatical-gender-distributional-semantics. We establish new minimum characteristic values for which certain general arithmetic groups become rigidly structured.  Specifically, we derive the following: 
For $n \geq 3$, the arithmeticity in algebraic groups over fields with more than one element occurs at a minimum characteristic of $2n+3$. 
Additionally, the multiplicative group of integers localized to a hyperbolic 3-dimensional lattice becomes rigidly structured at a minimum characteristic of $8$. 
The given results combine novel applications of "charminity" - a theoretical concept recently developed - with well-established rigidity theorems. 
Notably, the theoretical underpinnings of charminity are still evolving, leaving current estimates for its implications partially predictive. 
The research aims to continue using charminity to provide estimates for the minimum characteristic at which generalized arithmetic groups become rigidly structured. 
A related finding related to charminity is included in an additional contribution to knowledge. 
To facilitate further exploration, a detailed collection of questions involving charminity and minimum characteristic at its current state of understanding are provided.

Estimating the precise 3D location of objects within images is a fundamental
goal in both computer vision and robotics. While current approaches typically
involve labeling individual images to train models capable of predicting object
positions, our research explores the possibility of making class-level position
estimation decisions without acquiring new data for each image or each class. 
A straightforward extension of existing localization methods would require
collecting new data for each image, greatly increasing the required amount
of data. In our study, a zero-shot and multi-output regression approach is
presented, addressing a simplified version of this issue by avoiding the need
for new data collection. Performance evaluation on the SUN360 dataset confirms
the benefits of this method. A related issue, estimating the positions of individual
objects within pairs consisting of an image and a 360-degree panorama, is
also investigated and a novel benchmark, the CPDataset, is created to address
this problem. Ultimately, our approach yields superior results on the CPDataset. 
Performance comparisons on the CPDataset reveal that our existing method
achieves similar results as a direct object-rotation method would, with the
added benefit of reduced noise. In particular, our existing method exhibits
well-balanced performance across rotational and positional accuracy, whereas
the direct approach exhibits improved rotational but inferior positional accuracy. 
It's also demonstrated that the direct approach experiences significant
degradation when applying the model to novel pairs consisting of images and
360-degree panoramas. A related problem, estimating the positions of individual
objects within pairs consisting of images and 360-degree panoramas, is 
investigated and a novel benchmark, the CPDataset, is created to address
this problem. Ultimately, our approach yields superior results on the CPDataset.

Our research reveals that movies from larger studios enjoy higher box office draws, but the actual box office total also heavily depends on the date and time of the film's domestic release. Furthermore, this investigation presents new information regarding box office earning predictors, including how domestic and international box office earnings correlate. The findings suggest that there are distinct characteristics of domestic and international box office earning models, and that a multi-linear model better captures box office earning variability. Consequently, this work proposes a combined system for predicting box office earnings that considers both film and studio-specific traits. As an added benefit, this study also evaluates how the features used in this model, inherited from pre-existing film attributes, influence box office earning predictions. Our analysis indicates that while certain features are found to have an impact, the addition of these extra variables does not significantly improve box office earning forecasts beyond the capacity of the combined system alone. Consequently, this work advocates for a combination of system features, by merging essential attributes from both domestic and international box office earning models. As a result, this study presents a unified system for predicting box office earnings that is versatile, efficient, and might be expanded upon in the future. Importantly, this combined system operates effectively at any scale, whether for a specific country's or the global box office, making it a valuable resource for filmmakers and industry analysts. Consequently, this study presents a unified system for predicting box office earnings that is beneficial to various stakeholders in the film industry. Auxiliary frequency regulation plays a crucial role in modern power grids and 
voltage stability is a key aspect of this function. We examine the voltage 
behavior under auxiliary frequency regulation in a particular context where 
the network and connected generators adhere to specific characteristics. We 
investigate the local dynamics of the voltage near the equilibrium state and 
demonstrate that it exhibits a limit cycle when certain conditions are met. We 
also discuss the implications of our findings for small-scale low-voltage grid 
operations. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that auxiliary frequency 
regulation can compromise voltage stability. We visually illustrate our 
conclusions using simulated examples. A web-based interactive tool enables 
users to explore these examples in greater depth. This research sheds light on 
voltage behavior within small-scale grids and may inform similar studies in 
larger power grid systems. We also suggest additional investigations into the 
local dynamics of power grid voltage. We address a particular shortcoming in 
existing theories of power grid dynamics by studying the behavior of voltages 
near equilibrium states and investigating the local properties of power-to-voltage 
transducers. We identify specific auxiliaries that can help stabilize 
voltage behavior but also introduce conditions under which voltage instability 
occurs. We illustrate a local phase-lock effect, which contributes to voltage 
instability. We examine the impact of auxiliary frequency regulation on voltage 
stability, revealing that it may actually decrease rather than increase it. We 
visualize limit cycle behavior near equilibrium states and show how phase-lock 
phase transitions lead to a local and (non)stable voltage behavior. We also 
investigate factors that contribute to such transitions. We believe our 
research improves current power grid dynamics understanding and may have practical 
applications for small-scale grid operators. We also hope that future studies 
can expand our analysis to larger power grid systems. We have attempted to make 
our analysis accessible to a broad audience by providing clear and detailed 
explanations, rather than solely relying on mathematical equations. We have also 
incorporated interactive elements for readers who prefer more engaging content.

These primordial magnetic fields not only played a role in regulating cosmic magnetic orders but also generated gravitational waves through the curvature-induced breakdown of magnetic knots. Notably, this gravitational wave signal has a frequency lower than the millisecond range and may be detectable by future pulsar timing array experiments. The PGW spectrum displays double power patterns, mirroring the features seen in the CMB, with variations dependent on the degree of magnetic disorder and initial conditions. The analysis assumes an isotropic distribution of magnetic knots without the effects of large-scale magnetic orders. In cross-language information retrieval, users can employ vector-based and similarity-metric approaches to locate equivalent documents across languages.  Two emerging frameworks, interactive and non-interactive, respectively leverage user interaction and do not necessitate it.  We studied the benefits of combining these frameworks in a single, unified approach to boost retrieval efficiency and effectiveness.  Our research centered on vector-based models, exploring how interactive and non-interactive frameworks compare and complement one another.  We observed that, while non-interactive frameworks perform better with less noisy data, interactive frameworks excelled with noisy data.  To combine these benefits, we developed a new approach, the Hybrid Cross-Language Information Retrieval Model, incorporating short passages and multi-paragraphs in a way that capitalizes on interactive relevance feedback for cleaner data and leverages non-interactive short passages for noisy input.  The model performed exceptionally well in our experiments and surpassed the current state-of-the-art on cross-lingual retrieval datasets.  Detailed analysis and assessment revealed our model's robustness across various levels of noise and data lengths, making it well-suited for multi-paragraph and multi-sentence datasets.  We have made the model public, enabling the community to utilize it for cross-lingual retrieval tasks.  Furthermore, our model's underlying mechanics can be applied to resolve other information retrieval challenges.  To facilitate seamless deployment, we have created a user-friendly web interface to facilitate quick and efficient cross-lingual retrieval.  The final model's details are available at https://github.com/harshgore and will be publicly released soon on HuggingFace's model hub.  A demonstration of the model can be found at https://clir-demos.github.io. The model has also received recognition through being selected as the winner of the 2022 Crosslingual Information Retrieval Challenge at the 2022 Semantic Evaluation Exercises (SemEval-2022). simulations. By representing the prestellar core as a free-standing core without external
infalls, the process of accretion is solely driven by heat release and radiative losses. When
core mass accumulation rates are calculated, they differ significantly from those derived
from standard models, often resulting in overestimation of the core's mass growth rate for
the early stages. In the standard models, the core's mass is estimated by balancing accretion
and external infalls, but this is equivalent to ignoring the core's nucleus rupture energy,
which is an essential component of the core's mass accumulation rate. Consequently, the
standard models suggest that the core's mass growth rate increases with mass, which is
impossible given the core's nucleus structure. In the core's early stages, the nucleus's
disintegration energy exceeds the accreted energy, slowing down the core's mass growth rate,
which becomes independent of mass and near constant. The disintegration energy is then
absorbed, and the core's accretion resumes, but with a lower rate. Furthermore, the core's
structure evolves, and the radiative boundary temperature increases, leading to a shift in
the core's internal and external mass fractions, which affect the core's mass accumulation rate
in the subsequent stages. The findings suggest that the core's mass growth rate for the
intermediate stages is lower than that of the standard models, whereas in the final stages,
the core's mass growth rate for the protostellar phase is higher than that of the standard
models, which is driven by the core's internal and external mass fractions and nucleus
energy. The outcome of these factors indicates that the core's mass distribution between the
external material and the protoplanetary disk is significantly influenced by the rupture of the
nucleus, which should be taken into consideration when determining the core's mass
accumulation rates. The resulting protoplanetary disk development from the free-standing core
to the Class-0 stage is significantly faster than that of the standard models, which suggest
that the formation of the Class-0 phase should be from a more massive prestellar core than
initially thought. The rapid evolution from the free-standing core to the protoplanetary disk
phase could be observed in the near future with the help of the James Webb Space Telescope.

Federated learning allows diverse parties to jointly develop a predictive model without sharing individual client data, which is in line with the principles of justice and data protection laws. Research has initially concentrated on justifying the legal applicability of these principles in the context of federated learning, whereas the feasibility and consequences of adopting these principles in practice have received less attention. We focus on achieving differential privacy, which is a common measure of data protection. We present two formal measures of achievable privacy: a low-data-disadvantage and a high-data-advantage. We show that a DPA can be thought of as a combination of two optimal PDPs for mutual benefit under certain conditions, which are also relevant for understanding the effects of data privacy measures in fair multi-party collaborative federated training. We also present a new interpretation of the fairness of the model training (fair risk allocation) under differential privacy and investigate whether the fairness and privacy can be simultaneously improved through simultaneous DPA pursuit. Additionally, we present a general method for maximizing the privacy benefits (LDDA) for models trained in a distributed manner by taking the derivative of the privacy objective function in relation to the local data distributed by the parties, which is also achievable via convex optimization. We demonstrate this method's effectiveness using real-world datasets and a predictive model. We observe that our LDDA solution for the private model exhibits both better classification performance and higher privacy benefits compared to the existing DPA solution. Interestingly, this method also yields a beneficial fairness outcome (fairer model), which cannot be replicated by the existing DPA solution. We observe that our LDDA solution exhibits improved consistency in its outcomes, which may lead to enhanced model transferability in contrast to the existing DPA. Additionally, we present two additional potential applications of our LDDA method beyond private FL, which include generalizing it to distributed optimization and developing a personalized recommendation system. We provide additional analysis and findings from these additional use cases in the full paper. We demonstrate these additional use cases in the full paper as well as present a video summary of our work at https://youtu.be/GS5Kqo6eY1E. Object detection is a fundamental problem in computer vision, but the traditional approach of training detection models using bounding-box annotations is costly as it demands label each object in every training image. To break this cost barrier, we introduce a novel method for training object detection models using a lexicon as a guide, based on a new type of annotation called pseudo bounding-box. By utilizing pseudo bounding-box annotations derived from word lists, we can train models directly without any image-level labels, making the process much more efficient. Our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art and sets a new standard for training object detection models using a lexicon, achieving this breakthrough without any additional supervision. Our research shows that pseudo bounding-box annotations can be reliable and accurate, performing on par with manually labeled bounds in our experiments. Additionally, we found that pseudo annotations derived from various synsets of a lexicon produce models with improved performance, indicating a connection between synset-related bounds and model performance. Our method's success also highlights the potential for further improving word detection limits using additional resources, such as sentence images and bounding box labels. Implementing this additional supervision, we were able to further improve our method's performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in our experiments. Our proposed technique and additional supervision method's source code and a dataset with pseudo annotations derived from synsets 5056 are publicly available at https://github.com/amberfang/lexicon_object_detection. Our research's findings were presented at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo (ICME). Notably, while our training pipeline leverages pseudo annotations for efficiency, our testing process relies on precise bounding-box labels, similar to the original Open Lexicon Object Identification method. To validate the pseudo annotations' effectiveness, we conducted multiple cross-distribution evaluation experiments, demonstrating that pseudo annotations derived from a lexicon's synsets can be reliable and accurate. Our research's findings indicate that pseudo annotations have the potential to train object detection models directly from an lexicon at a significantly reduced cost, eliminating the need for image-level labels. Implementing additional supervision, such as cross-camera training or bounding-box labels across images, can further improve our method's performance and bring it in line with state-of-the-art results, making it suitable for production environments. Advanced econometric techniques such as factor analysis have become essential 
in understanding complex data sets and addressing issues of excess information.
The advanced method of stochastic differential equations combined with data-driven state space models 
offers refined factor analysis, enabling the incorporation of common factor variations 
over time, which is crucial in managing financial institutions and healthcare systems. 
These systems involve combining individual units (financial institutions or patients), 
each with unique characteristics (factor loadings), into homogeneous groups (factor groups). 
The behavior within these groups may change over time due to various policies or interventions. 
Therefore, the traditional static factor model, which assumes fixed factor loadings, might not be sufficient. 
We present a dynamic factor model framework, where the factor loadings evolve according to given differential equations, 
which can be applied to patient data sets using a numerical state-space model, 
enabling the prediction of future patient mortality. 

We showcase the effectiveness of the proposed model through numerical simulations and real-world data analysis using patient information from the University of Michigan Health System. 
The results demonstrate that considering time-varying factor loadings significantly improves patient mortality prediction accuracy. 
Compared to static and independently evolving factor loadings models, 
the proposed model provides more accurate forecasts and reliable estimates with lower volatility. 
Furthermore, the proposed approach allows for the smooth evolution of factor loadings, 
which aligns with clinical expert insights that adjustments are gradual and typically occur 
in response to substantial interventions such as introducing antibiotics for sepsis patients. 

Using real-world data, we evaluate the ability of each model to predict patient mortality, 
including cases of sepsis, septic shock, sepsis septic shock, urinary tract infections, 
pneumonia, transient urinary tract infections, transient urinary tract infections with pneumonia, 
and chest pain. The results reveal that incorporating time-varying factor loadings leads to enhanced predictive performance, 
resulting in significantly more deaths being predicted as mortality risk increases. 
The proposed model also outperforms the other models as mortality forecast accuracy grows with time. 
Ultimately, the proposed stochastic differential equation-state space model offers reliable mortality predictions and patient outcome forecasts. 

Using real-world data from the University of Michigan Health System, 
the proposed approach allows for the simulation of patient outcomes before admission, 
enabling the selection of patients with the highest risk of mortality. 
The proposed model also offers reliable forecasts of future mortality, 
alongside the selection of most likely diagnoses and treatments.

Neural architecture search (NAS) effectively automates the architecture development process but is constrained due to the disruption phenomenon, which causes nascent models to rapidly switch between potential candidates, hindering thorough exploration and time-efficient discovery of superior architectures. To tackle this issue, researchers have proposed using residual connections and incorporating multi-step look-ahead structures into the search process. However, current approaches only partially address the disruption problem, and their designs are often empirically determined. In contrast, this study presents a theoretically founded framework for NAS that addresses the root causes of disruption. By reformulating NAS as a control problem, this framework leverages the policy gradient method to train a search space navigator that expertly guides the selection of models. Experimental results demonstrate that the trained navigator significantly outperforms existing solutions by tailoring the selection process to specific models and applications. Consequently, models optimized by the trained navigator exhibit enhanced performance on multiple fronts, as evidenced by our experiments with various architectures and datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios. Notably, our optimized models match or surpass the performance of human-designed architectures and leading NAS methods, including NASNet and AutoML, often by a considerable margin. Furthermore, our trained navigator successfully identifies top-performing models that had been previously overlooked, indicating that disruption can be fully alleviated through targeted control. Importantly, our findings highlight the considerable potential for further improvement if NAS is instead focused on discovering diverse, well-adapted models rather than solely seeking to identify the architecture with the highest validation accuracy. To facilitate the further development of NAS, we release the trained navigator and related code to the public domain through our repository. By empowering NAS to explore a broader range of architectures using a more informed and efficient search process, our proposed control problem framework represents a significant step forward in the architecture search space. Recent studies have applied the principles of quantum coherence and energy conservation to derive sum rules for the coherent absorption of light. Specifically, this work examines the relationship between metric tensors in different coordinate systems used in quantum scattering theory. We demonstrate that coordinate changes lead to specific constraints when evaluating metric tensors. Notably, this requires that the sum of individual elements representing different directions from a reference point must be zero. Furthermore, we clarify that proper change-of-variable matrices preserve sign. These constraints are then applied to derive coherent absorption eigenchannels in terms of generalized scattering amplitude. An example illustration uses a two-dimensional polarization state. The mathematical framework developed here is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of situations, including those involving multiple spatial dimensions and vast, high-dimensional spaces. Specifically, this approach can be used to derive eigenchannels for coherent absorption in systems with up to n-dimensional polarization states. Moreover, our calculations based on the metric determinant rather than individual elements have the benefit of not being overly influenced by large dimensional values. We support our analytical findings with corresponding numerical evidence. Ultimately, this work provides a foundation for exploring eigenchannels in diverse scattering environments covered by this metric-shift framework. Specifically, this framework can be used to analyze problems related to coherent absorption, including scenarios involving multiple-pulse interactions with matter. Metrics that fall under this category have been used to study these complex interactions. For instance, previous studies have applied this approach to the issue of double optical injection lock, a conceptually simple model that helps to better understand the underlying physics of multi-pulse interactions. We anticipate that the framework and analysis provided in this paper will be valuable for investigating a wide range of complex interactions in quantum systems. Furthermore, we have previously demonstrated that the scattering framework is equivalent to a type of quantum diffusion process. Using this approach, we have calculated various physical metrics, including the Froude number, Reynolds number, and Rayleigh number, in terms of scattering amplitude. We have also applied the scattering framework to the issue of quantum fractals, which has traditionally been studied using self-similar mathematical concepts. An alternative approach grounded in scattering theory yields similar results as the fractal method, but with less difficulty. Notably, we have used the scattering framework to derive a coherent absorption principle that does not rely on the concept of dimension. Instead, the coherence has the potential to transcend traditional dimensional boundaries. We examine how best to train standard, fully-connected neural networks, using standard optimization methods, by analyzing the development of high-performing sub-networks, or "winning lottery tickets," within these networks. Our analysis discovers that these winning tickets often emerge early in training, similar to those found in feedforward neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, often developing by the point when the loss first begins to decline. Notably, continuing to train these tickets without adjusting any parameters results in a significant decline of their effectiveness within the first hundred training steps. Our research suggests that convolutional neural networks may maintain an advantage over fully-connected neural networks due to their ability to effectively eliminate unimportant connections. Based on these findings, we propose a novel "trimming" algorithm which effectively removes unimportant connections from a fully-connected neural network by converting them to skip connections. Furthermore, we develop mathematical models that quantify the intensity and likelihood of such instances, and we show that these instances can be highly plausible, even within the training data's normal distribution. At the same time, we also identify upper limits to the severity and frequency of potential threats, which are influenced by various factors, including the complexity and accuracy of the quantum classifier, the number of available training data, and the characteristics of the underlying data distribution. Several models have been developed to forecast global energy consumption growth, 
although there is a lack of systematic research on model evaluation in this area. 
This paper investigates and addresses two key questions: How can we assess the 
accuracy of such models? and Can we identify models that outperform others? 
To answer these questions, we propose a novel evaluation framework that uses 
multiple scoring methods to analyze residual errors from simulated runs. 
By applying our framework to a dataset of 11 models, we find that most models 
tend to overestimate energy consumption growth during the initial growth phase, 
but underestimate it in the later, more mature phase. Furthermore, we cannot 
conclusively determine the best model due to varying model performances 
depending on the forecasting interval and method used. However, models that 
utilize aggregate variables such as energy intensity or energy intensity growth 
tend to provide more accurate forecasts compared to those models that do 
not incorporate these variables. This research highlights the importance of 
residual error analysis in evaluating and comparing economic growth models. 
Moreover, it reveals the potential issues with models that are based on 
assumptions grounded in theoretical knowledge but may not align with empirical 
realities. This insight can be applied not only to energy consumption models but 
also to other areas of predictive modeling. Finally, we suggest a focus on 
developing more precise models that can simulate growth phases in a more 
accurate manner.

Most concept-based search approaches rely on keyword-based queries, and identifying these keywords, or search phrases, is essential. Researchers have previously explored automatic search phrase identification, but most existing methods are unsupervised and evaluate their performance using search relevance as a secondary consideration. This paper proposes a new supervised method that evaluates a set of potential search phrases based on both their relevance and position. We introduce a new metric called the "retrieved search phrase score," and a method called "Search Phrase Inference Through Retrieval Given Concepts" (STRICT), which uses a retrieval-based approach to identify the most relevant search phrases for a given query. We test STRICT on a substantial dataset of human-annotated search phrases and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing unsupervised methods. Furthermore, we show that our proposed method not only outperforms previous approaches but also achieves better results than some supervised methods in terms of concept placement. We also improve the computational efficiency of STRICT, allowing it to handle large datasets and widely-used evaluation metrics. The proposed approach and evaluation process are valid within the given dataset and can be adapted to other datasets with similar characteristics. We believe this research can contribute to the development of more accurate and efficient concept-based search methods. We propose that the hydrodynamic disturbances in the dissipation range of turbulent flows originate from the movement of molecules, which is an aspect of fluid dynamics typically overlooked. This mechanism is similar to how thermal energy gives rise to random fluctuations in equilibrium states - the Nernst heat vector emerges, driving thermal disturbances that create fluctuations in the dissipation range. Consequently, the intensity of these fluctuations is expected to be proportional to $T^2$ and $L^{-1}$. Additionally, we provide potential explanations for the local balance between turbulent kinetic energy and shear stress in the dissipation range, citing the role of eddies with sizes of approximately 10-20 times the Kolmogorov scale in this phenomenon. Furthermore, we suggest that the resilience of the turbulent flow to increased temperature within this range is indicative of an energy transfer from the inner eddies to the outer ones. This is an anomaly, as the outer eddies typically experience increased forward transfer of energy with rising temperature, which we attribute to the inner eddies assuming a critical state near the estimated minimum for liquid turbulence. This state is characterized by the condition that $u_{\infty}^2 < 3\mu (\partial U/ \partial x)$. When this condition is met, an additional forward transfer of energy takes place - until this requirement is fulfilled, the turbulent flow shows signs of decay. The proposed mechanism is expected to facilitate a deeper understanding of the turbulent dissipation process and potentially be applied to other fields, such as biological systems and planetary science. It may also help explain phenomena observed in studies of turbulent flows, including the apparent negative value of the second Heywood number $I_2 = -\overline{w\partial \tilde{u}/\partial z}$. Furthermore, future research could verify the existence of these minimal states for homogeneous, anisotropic turbulence and examine the effect of variations within these states, given that they are expected to significantly influence turbulent dissipation and potentially offer a way to quantify turbulent states using molecular movement. The concept of these minimal states could also be applied to non-isotropic, three-dimensional turbulent flows, potentially shedding light on their structure and helping to reconcile the balance requirements within the dissipation range. It could also reveal the underlying physical mechanism driving the formation of these states and the factors influencing their shape and size. Ultimately, these states could help to explain why certain factors affect turbulent dissipation when included in dissipation rate formulas, despite seemingly having no connection to this process. Recent findings from long-term observations of CR Draconis, a binary system consisting of two flare stars, support the hypothesis that its low-frequency radiation originates from an electron-cyclotron maser mechanism. Over a period of nearly five years, scheduled observations captured 75 out of 81 possible epochs, revealing a distinctive "double-peaked" characteristic in the radio spectrum at low frequencies. The persistent and steady radiation pattern suggests that the underlying process is stable. Modeling the spectrum using a magnetized electron-hydrodynamic source, in conjunction with a Faraday rotation mechanism, yields optimal parameters for matching observed spectra. The proposed mechanism is consistent with observed patterns in CR Draconis and comparable to those seen in red dwarf binaries AR Draconis and AD Leonis, both of which also display stable, low-frequency radiation. 

Please note that this article builds upon a previously published study in the Journal of Atmospheric and Solar-Terrestrial Physics (2020), in addition to presenting new findings obtained in 2020. The observed characteristics in CR Draconis in this article overlap with those present in the initial study, which covers a broader period from 2011 to 2018.

The existing methods for 3D reconstruction and relighting in the area have shown promising results, yet they fail to produce a realistic and coherent 2D image of the 3D reconstructed avatar. This work introduces a novel and efficient technique for 2D and 3D alignment known as Neural Separation, one that separates the luminance, color, and shape of the input image from its 3D geometry. The results of our method have demonstrated the ability to produce photorealistic images of manipulated avatars, as well as a range of applications including virtual try-on, 3D animation, and editing of self-portraits. Recent breakthroughs in Zero-shot Natural Language Inference (ZSNLI) have been achieved by pre-trained language models, which can perform the task without relying on explicit training, relying solely on the use of a standard dataset and a given prompt to yield a high performance score. Nonetheless, further analysis has shown that a substantial portion of the prompt is often missing, taking the form of information assembled from the training data sets, which was absent from the initial experiments. Our study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by conducting a comprehensive meta-analysis of the interactions between datasets and prompts that were overlooked in previous studies. Our findings indicate that a significant degree of diversity exists in the combinations of datasets and prompts used in Zero-shot tasks and that there is a universal tendency to prioritize a limited number of popular dataset and prompt assemblies that happen to deliver satisfactory results, which may lead to suboptimal performance when encountered with other combinations. To address this issue, we conducted a series of meta-tuning experiments on the GPT2 and BERT4, allowing them to generalize their knowledge to a broader set of prompt assemblies. Our results demonstrate that their performance improves notably on out-of-scope prompts, which opens up a wealth of potential Zero-shot NLI solutions waiting to be discovered. Theoretical and lattice investigations of a $SU(3)-$Higgs model have yielded results that reveal a limitation-deactivation phase transition. This previously unidentified phenomenon occurs when the Higgs boson's mass approaches the mass of a $W$ boson from below. Upon deactivation, the center symmetry is broken continuously, resulting in the formation of multiple stable minima in the energy landscape. These minima stem from the appearance of continuously broken $SU(3)/U(3)$ axes, which emerge due to a limitation-deactivation phase transition caused by the disappearance of $W$-mass tunings and the emergence of Higgs-mass tunings. Limitation-deactivation phase transitions may be generalizable to other theories featuring dynamical mass generation. Moreover, such phase transitions could be identifiable through observations of $W$-mass tunings in experiments involving high-energy collisions at the LHC and future hadron colliders. This could be achieved by analyzing certain patterns of four- and five-jet production that become evident at linear collider energies. Notably, these limitation-deactivation phase transitions differ from known deconstruction-deactivation phase transitions in $U(1)-$Higgs models. Research suggests that Deconfinement limit-deactivation phase transitions may occur both in the Deconfinement phase and when there's no supercooling involved. Wildfires pose a significant threat to global ecosystems, and efficient detection and monitoring are crucial for managing them. Satellite imagery, by providing timely and detailed information on wildfires as they evolve, is vital for research and response efforts. By fusing visible and thermal images of the same region, researchers can create comprehensive visual representations of wildfires that facilitate more effective detection, monitoring, and analysis. Nevertheless, combining these images often results in poor quality due to the inherent differences between visible and thermal imaging. Consequently, the visual integration of these images has been restricted in the past. Advances in deep learning have empowered the processing of unique patterns in thermal imaging and the integration of mixed-mode datasets. As a result, the incorporation of thermal data within deep learning models can enhance the detection and classification capabilities for wildfires. Our proposed model, FIRe-GAN, utilizes a generative adversarial network approach to seamlessly integrate visible and thermal images, yielding high-quality combined datasets. By incorporating these integrated datasets into a semantic segmentation network, we observed substantial enhancements in wildfire detection and visualization. The creation of novel datasets through FIRe-GAN has the potential to empower researchers in computer vision to develop more efficient techniques for detecting and analyzing wildfires. Ultimately, the proposed model outperformed existing methods in terms of accuracy and FIO scores, which are critical metrics in this domain. Our research paves the path for future researchers to develop more effective wildfire detection and visualization algorithms. The integrated datasets, named FIRe-GAN-DS, and source codes, named FIRe-GAN-SC, are now publicly available. By advancing the detection and visualization capabilities for wildfires, our research promotes the discovery of new insights in wildfire dynamics. These insights, in turn, can foster the development of more efficient algorithms to estimate the severity and intensity of upcoming wildfires. The investigation into mental health crises enabled by data analysis is growing, with a focus on identifying signs of depression through social media discussion trends. 

However, the process of compiling relevant data, assessing its quality, and empirically testing indicators on larger datasets remains largely unexplored. 

In this study, we explain the process of gathering social media data relevant to depression, examining our dataset's characteristics, and outlining the design of our study. 

We discovered several data challenges during our research, including uneven posting frequencies and uneven word distributions in our dataset. 

We have therefore developed a data-driven method for automatically generating depression-related datasets from social media platforms. 

We empirically compared four automatic methods for identifying depression indicators: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency, Latent Dirichlet Allocation, Doc2Vec, and Word Embedding. 

Our findings reveal that combining two of these methods enables superior performance to human-labeled benchmarks on larger social media datasets. 

Ultimately, we propose a hybrid approach combining Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency and Latent Dirichtlet Allocation for identifying depression indicators on large social media datasets and open-source our dataset for the research community. 

Our research findings and dataset can be found at: https://github.com/Minisky/Depression-Indicators-Research. 

This research aims to stimulate further investigation into the process of gathering social media data, assessing its quality, and empirically testing indicators on larger datasets.

We present a novel regularization technique called Profound Bellman Risk Management (ProBM), designed for model-based reinforcement learning (RL) to limit the maximum expected value of policy gradients. ProBM offers a range of benefits, including improving model representational quality, stabilizing model and controller training, enhancing resilience to optimisation difficulties, and reducing the impact of noisy data in synthetic RL. Our approach builds on the notion of Bellman risk from \cite{ezran2020bellman}, utilizing a recursive formula and a trainable encoder to impose a universal Lipschitz constraint on the Bellman operator. Notably, ProBM's encoder can function as a pre-trained model for downstream synthetic RL tasks, saving time and reducing the requirement for task-specific data. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that, under certain conditions, ProBM yields a tight, data-dependent upper bound on the Bellman expectation value. Our experimental findings confirm that ProBM yields consistent results and outperforms traditional RL methods, especially in scenarios with noisy data. Furthermore, our assessment of ProBM's scalability reveals its capacity to handle complex control problems efficiently. Overall, our results illustrate the efficacy of ProBM in mitigating excessive Bellman expectation values and enhancing model and controller performance.
